Debug toFQDNs Policy Not Matching anihpj External API Calls

The Problem: anihpj needs to call api.github.com for OAuth. A toFQDNs CNP is applied but all HTTPS requests to api.github.com time out. DNS resolves, but traffic is DROPPED. The FQDN rule doesn't match.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600

cat > cnbug.yaml << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-github-oauth
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  egress:
  - toEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns, "io.kubernetes.pod.namespace": kube-system}}]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "53", protocol: UDP}]}]
  - toFQDNs:
    - matchName: "api.github.com"      # ❌ BUG: matchName = exact — GitHub uses CNAME chain!
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "443", protocol: TCP}]}]
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnbug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Pod Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → web Running ✅
✓2. DNS works: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- nslookup api.github.com → resolved ✅
✗3. HTTPS blocked: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget --timeout=3 https://api.github.com → TIMEOUT! ❌
✗4. Hubble DROPPED: hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED → HTTPS to GitHub IPs DROPPED ❌
✗5. FQDN cache mismatch: cilium fqdn cache list → GitHub returns multiple IPs via CNAME ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check FQDN rule: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj allow-github-oauth -o yaml | grep -A5 toFQDNs
→ matchName: "api.github.com" — exact match only
2Check DNS resolution chain: nslookup api.github.com → CNAME to github.map.fastly.net → multiple A records
→ matchName fails because the resolved IPs don't trace back to the exact matchName!
3Use matchPattern instead: matchPattern supports wildcard patterns like *.github.com to cover CNAME chains
4Hubble confirms: hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED -o json | jq '.flow.destination_names' → IPs resolved but not matching FQDN
5Root cause identified: matchName requires exact DNS name match — CNAME chains cause mismatch; use matchPattern with wildcard
🔧

🔧 Fix — Change matchName to matchPattern for CNAME Coverage

BASH
kubectl delete cnp -n anihpj allow-github-oauth
kubectl apply -f - << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-github-oauth
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  egress:
  - toEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns, "io.kubernetes.pod.namespace": kube-system}}]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "53", protocol: UDP}]}]
  - toFQDNs:
    - matchPattern: "*.github.com"
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "443", protocol: TCP}]}]
CNP
✓

✅ Verify — GitHub OAuth API Reachable

After switching to matchPattern: *.github.com, all GitHub subdomains in the CNAME chain are covered. wget https://api.github.com returns HTTP 200. hubble observe shows FORWARDED HTTPS traffic.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
FQDN rule blocks traffic
②
matchName = exact
③
CNAME chain breaks match
④
Use matchPattern wildcard
⑤
GitHub API reachable

Tenet: matchName requires an exact DNS name match. When services use CNAME chains (like GitHub → Fastly CDN), the resolved IPs may not trace back to the matchName. Use matchPattern with wildcards for services behind CDNs.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 https://api.github.com wget: download timed out ← FQDN rule not matching
$ cilium fqdn cache list FQDN TTL IPs api.github.com 300 140.82.121.5, 140.82.121.6 ← IPs resolved but matchName fails on CNAME chain
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED -o json | jq '.flow.destination_names' ["api.github.com"] ← DNS name present but policy drops
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 https://api.github.com HTTP 200 OK ✅ GitHub OAuth reachable
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict FORWARDED --to-fqdn github.com TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION VERDICT 12:08:01 web-xxx 140.82.121.5:443 FORWARDED ✅

Enable Policy Audit Mode and Verify with Hubble Observe on anihpj

The Problem: You want to test a new deny policy before enforcing it. You enable audit mode, but Hubble shows FORWARDED instead of AUDIT. The policy appears to be enforcing when it should only be auditing.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine

# ❌ BUG: Applied policy in default mode (enforcing) instead of audit mode
cat > cnbug.yaml << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: test-deny-egress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  egress:
  - toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "53", protocol: UDP}]}]
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnbug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Pod Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → web and api Running ✅
✓2. CNP applied: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj → test-deny-egress exists ✅
✗3. Traffic DROPPED instead of audited: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget --timeout=3 http://1.1.1.1 → TIMEOUT! ❌ (should pass in audit!)
✗4. Hubble shows DROPPED not AUDIT: hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED → DROPPED instead of audited! ❌
✗5. cilium policy get shows enforcement: cilium policy get → enforcement mode: default ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check enforcement mode: cilium policy get | head -5
→ Policy Enforcement Mode: default — enforcing, not auditing!
2Understand audit mode: cilium config PolicyEnforcementMode=audit sets global audit mode — policy evaluated but NOT enforced
3Current behavior: Policy is in enforcing mode — traffic is actually DROPPED, not just reported
4Hubble verification: In audit mode, Hubble shows verdict as "audit" with FORWARDED traffic — currently shows DROPPED
5Root cause identified: PolicyEnforcementMode not set to audit — policy is enforcing instead of auditing
🔧

🔧 Fix — Enable Audit Mode, Test, Then Re-Enable Enforcement

BASH
cilium config PolicyEnforcementMode=audit
sleep 3
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://1.1.1.1
hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict FORWARDED -o json | jq '.flow.policy_match_type'
# After testing, re-enable enforcement:
cilium config PolicyEnforcementMode=default
✓

✅ Verify — Hubble Shows AUDIT Instead of DROPPED

After setting PolicyEnforcementMode=audit, traffic passes through but Hubble reports policy_match_type: audit. The policy is evaluated and logged but NOT enforced. This allows safe testing before enforcement.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Traffic dropped → not auditing
②
Check enforcement mode → default
③
Set to audit mode
④
Hubble shows audit verdict
⑤
Test safely → re-enable

Tenet: Cilium audit mode evaluates policies and reports verdicts via Hubble, but does NOT enforce them. Set PolicyEnforcementMode=audit globally to test policies safely before enforcing. Hubble shows policy_match_type: audit for audited flows.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)

$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://1.1.1.1 wget: download timed out ← Actually DROPPED, should pass in audit
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED -o json | jq '.flow.policy_match_type' "enforced" ← Enforced, not audited
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict FORWARDED -o json | jq '.flow.policy_match_type' "audit" ✅ Policy evaluated but NOT enforced — safe testing
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://1.1.1.1 HTTP 200 OK ✅ Traffic passes in audit mode, policy only reports
$ cilium policy get | head -3 Policy Enforcement Mode: audit ✅ Audit mode active for testing

🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Inspect CNP CIDR reference: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj allow-vpn -o yaml | grep -A3 fromCIDR
→ fromCIDR: [10.10.0.0/16] — hardcoded, missing 172.16.0.0/12!
2Check CIDRGroup exists: kubectl get ciliumcidrgroup office-vpn-ranges -o yaml
→ externalCIDRs: [10.10.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12] — both ranges defined
3Understand CIDRGroup referencing: CNP must use fromCIDRSet with cidrGroupRef to reference a CIDRGroup, not hardcoded fromCIDR
4Current CNP bypasses CIDRGroup: The CNP uses fromCIDR directly — the CIDRGroup is created but never used
5Root cause identified: CNP uses hardcoded fromCIDR instead of fromCIDRSet with cidrGroupRef — CIDRGroup is unused
🔧

🔧 Fix — Reference CIDRGroup via fromCIDRSet with cidrGroupRef

BASH
kubectl delete cnp -n anihpj allow-vpn
kubectl apply -f - << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-vpn
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromCIDRSet:
    - cidrGroupRef: "office-vpn-ranges"
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]}]
CNP
✓

✅ Verify — Both VPN Ranges Now Allowed

After switching to fromCIDRSet with cidrGroupRef, both VPN ranges are enforced. Traffic from 172.16.x.x and 10.10.x.x is FORWARDED. CIDRGroups centralize CIDR management across multiple policies.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
VPN 172.16 blocked
②
CNP hardcodes one CIDR
③
CIDRGroup has both ranges
④
Use fromCIDRSet + cidrGroupRef
⑤
Both ranges now work

Tenet: CiliumCIDRGroup centralizes CIDR definitions. CNPs reference them via fromCIDRSet.cidrGroupRef, not fromCIDR. This allows updating CIDRs in one place without modifying every policy.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get cnp -n anihpj allow-vpn -o yaml | grep -A3 fromCIDR fromCIDR: - 10.10.0.0/16 ← Only one range, 172.16 missing!
$ kubectl get ciliumcidrgroup office-vpn-ranges -o yaml | grep externalCIDRs -A3 externalCIDRs: - 10.10.0.0/16 - 172.16.0.0/12 ← Both defined but never referenced
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://api-service --interface 172.16.5.10 000 ← 172.16.x.x blocked — CIDRGroup not in use
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get cnp -n anihpj allow-vpn -o yaml | grep -A3 fromCIDRSet fromCIDRSet: - cidrGroupRef: office-vpn-ranges ✅ CIDRGroup referenced
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://api-service 200 ✅ Both VPN ranges now allowed via CIDRGroup
🧹

🧹 Cleanup

BASH
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

Fix Host Firewall CCNP Blocking SSH to anihpj Worker Nodes

The Problem: A Host Firewall CCNP was applied to secure worker nodes, but now SSH access to ALL worker nodes is blocked. Admins can't access nodes for maintenance. The policy is too restrictive.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine

cat > ccnp-bug.yaml << 'CCNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: host-firewall
spec:
  nodeSelector: {matchLabels: {}}
  ingress:
  - fromEntities: [cluster]         # ❌ BUG: Only cluster entity — SSH from external blocked!
CCNP
kubectl apply -f ccnp-bug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. CCNP applied: kubectl get ccnp → host-firewall exists ✅
✓2. Cluster-internal traffic works: pod-to-pod communication normal ✅
✗3. SSH from admin machine blocked: ssh worker-node-1 → Connection refused! ❌
✗4. Hubble shows SSH DROPPED: hubble observe --from-entity world --to-port 22 → DROPPED! ❌
✗5. No world entity allowed: kubectl get ccnp -o yaml | grep -c world → 0 ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check CCNP entities: kubectl get ccnp host-firewall -o yaml | grep -A3 fromEntities
→ fromEntities: [cluster] — only cluster, NO world!
2Understand host firewall scope: CCNP with nodeSelector controls traffic TO the node — SSH from external comes from 'world' entity
3Check SSH traffic in Hubble: hubble observe --from-entity world --to-port 22 --verdict DROPPED
→ All external SSH traffic DROPPED
4Missing external access: Need to add fromEntities: [world] with explicit port 22 for admin SSH access
5Root cause identified: Host firewall only allows 'cluster' entity — external SSH from 'world' entity is blocked
🔧

🔧 Fix — Add 'world' Entity with SSH Port to Host Firewall

BASH
kubectl delete ccnp host-firewall
kubectl apply -f - << 'CCNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: host-firewall
spec:
  nodeSelector: {matchLabels: {}}
  ingress:
  - fromEntities: [cluster]
  - fromEntities: [world]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "22", protocol: TCP}]}]
CCNP
✓

✅ Verify — SSH Access Restored, Cluster Traffic Unaffected

After adding fromEntities: [world] with TCP/22, admins can SSH to worker nodes. Cluster-internal traffic still flows. hubble observe shows FORWARDED for SSH from world entity.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
SSH blocked → host firewall
②
Only cluster entity allowed
③
SSH comes from world entity
④
Add world + port 22
⑤
SSH restored, cluster safe

Tenet: Host Firewall CCNPs using nodeSelector control ALL traffic to the node. External SSH originates from the world entity. Always include fromEntities: [world] with explicit port rules for admin access.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ ssh worker-node-1 ssh: connect to host worker-node-1 port 22: Connection refused ← SSH blocked
$ hubble observe --from-entity world --to-port 22 --verdict DROPPED TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION PORT VERDICT 12:01:01 192.168.1.50:34567 worker-1:22 22 DROPPED ← External SSH blocked by host firewall
$ kubectl get ccnp host-firewall -o yaml | grep -c world 0 ← No world entity in host firewall
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ ssh -o ConnectTimeout=3 worker-node-1 'echo OK' OK ✅ SSH access restored
$ hubble observe --from-entity world --to-port 22 --verdict FORWARDED TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION PORT VERDICT 12:05:01 192.168.1.50:34567 worker-1:22 22 FORWARDED ✅

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH

cat > cnbug.yaml << 'CNP'

kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: api}}]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "5432", protocol: TCP}]}]
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {}}]      # ❌ BUG: Empty matchLabels matches ALL pods!
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "5432", protocol: TCP}]}]
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnbug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → db and web Running ✅
✓2. CNP applied: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj → restrict-db exists ✅
✗3. Policy trace shows ALLOW for web→db: cilium policy trace --src-label app=web --dst-label app=db --dport 5432 → ALLOW! ❌
✗4. Web→db actually allowed: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- nc -zv db-ip 5432 → Connected! ❌
✗5. Two ingress rules: second rule with empty matchLabels allows everyone ❌

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Trace the policy: cilium policy trace --src-label app=web --dst-label app=db --dport 5432/tcp
→ Verdict: ALLOW — second ingress rule matches all pods!
2Inspect CNP rules: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj restrict-db -o yaml | grep -c fromEndpoints
→ 2 — two ingress rules, second with matchLabels: {}!
3Understand additive rules: Empty matchLabels: {} matches ALL pods — combined with first rule via OR logic
4Policy trace details: cilium policy trace --src-label app=web --dst-label app=db --dport 5432 -o json → Shows matching rule is the second one
5Root cause identified: Second ingress rule with empty matchLabels:{} acts as wildcard — allows all sources via OR logic
🔧

🔧 Fix — Remove the Wildcard Ingress Rule (Empty matchLabels)

BASH
kubectl patch cnp -n anihpj restrict-db --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/ingress/1"}]'

✅ Verify — Policy Trace Now Shows DENY for web→db

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Trace shows ALLOW → unexpected
②
Two ingress rules
③
Second has matchLabels:{}
④
Empty = wildcard match
⑤
Remove → trace shows DENY

Tenet: cilium policy trace simulates policy evaluation between endpoints. Multiple ingress rules combine with OR logic — an empty matchLabels: {} acts as a wildcard allowing all sources. Use trace to verify expected behavior before deploying.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ cilium policy trace --src-label app=web --dst-label app=db --dport 5432/tcp Verdict: ALLOW Matching Rule: restrict-db (ingress rule #2) ← ALLOW when DENY expected!
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- nc -zv -w3 10.0.1.10 5432 Connection succeeded ← Web can still reach db
$ kubectl get cnp -n anihpj restrict-db -o yaml | grep -c fromEndpoints 2 ← Two rules, second has empty matchLabels
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cilium policy trace --src-label app=web --dst-label app=db --dport 5432/tcp Verdict: DENY ✅ Correctly denied
$ cilium policy trace --src-label app=api --dst-label app=db --dport 5432/tcp Verdict: ALLOW Matching Rule: restrict-db (ingress rule #1) ✅ API still allowed
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- nc -zv -w3 10.0.1.10 5432 nc: connection timed out ✅ Web→db now blocked

Resolve L7 Policy Not Applying — Missing Proxy Redirection on anihpj

The Problem: You created an L7 CNP to filter HTTP paths on the API pod, but the L7 rules are completely ignored. All HTTP traffic passes through regardless of path or method. Hubble shows no L7 enforcement.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600

# ❌ BUG: L7 policy created but Envoy proxy not deployed — no L7 enforcement!
cat > cnbug.yaml << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-l7-filter
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: web}}]
    toPorts:
    - ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]
      rules:
        http:
        - method: GET
          path: "^/api/.*"
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnbug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → web and api Running ✅
✓2. CNP with L7 rules exists: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj → api-l7-filter ✅
✗3. L7 rules ignored: curl -X POST http://api-service/admin → HTTP 200! ❌ (should be blocked!)
✗4. Hubble shows no L7 enforcement: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json → no HTTP rule matching ❌
✗5. No Envoy proxy: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep cilium-envoy → No Envoy pods! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check for Envoy proxy: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=cilium-envoy
→ No Envoy pods found — L7 enforcement requires Envoy!
2Verify Cilium config: cilium config | grep -i envoy
→ envoy-config.enabled: false — Envoy proxy not enabled
3Understand L7 enforcement: Cilium L7 policies require Envoy proxy for HTTP/gRPC/Kafka parsing — without Envoy, L7 rules are silently ignored
4Hubble confirms: L4 forwarding works but L7 filtering doesn't — all HTTP methods/paths pass through
5Root cause identified: L7 policy requires Envoy proxy (cilium-envoy DaemonSet) — not deployed, so L7 rules silently ignored
🔧

🔧 Fix — Enable Envoy Proxy for L7 Enforcement

BASH
cilium upgrade --set envoy.enabled=true
kubectl rollout status daemonset cilium-envoy -n kube-system --timeout=120s
# Re-apply the L7 policy after Envoy is running
kubectl delete cnp -n anihpj api-l7-filter
kubectl apply -f - << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-l7-filter
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: web}}]
    toPorts:
    - ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]
      rules:
        http:
        - method: GET
          path: "^/api/.*"
CNP
✓

✅ Verify — L7 HTTP Rules Now Enforced

After deploying Envoy proxy, POST /admin returns 403 Forbidden while GET /api/health returns 200. hubble observe shows L7 HTTP rule matching with FORWARDED/DROPPED verdicts.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
L7 rules ignored → POST allowed
②
No Envoy proxy running
③
L7 requires Envoy for HTTP parsing
④
Enable Envoy via Helm
⑤
L7 enforcement now active

Tenet: Cilium L7 policies (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka) require Envoy proxy for protocol parsing. Without Envoy, L7 rules are silently ignored and all L4 traffic passes. Enable with --set envoy.enabled=true during Cilium installation.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X POST http://api-service/admin 200 ← POST /admin should be blocked by L7 rule!
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=cilium-envoy No resources found ← Envoy proxy not deployed
$ hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq '.flow.l7' null ← No L7 parsing — Envoy not running
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X POST http://api-service/admin 403 ✅ POST /admin blocked by L7 rule
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://api-service/api/health 200 ✅ GET /api/health allowed
$ hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq '.flow.l7.http.method, .flow.verdict' "POST" "DROPPED" ✅ L7 enforcement via Envoy proxy

✓2. Pod Running in anihpj: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → web Running ✅

🔧 Fix — Move CNP to the Correct Namespace (anihpj)

①

Policy in wrong namespace

CNP namespace ≠ pod namespace

Move to correct namespace

cilium policy get shows it

Debug Policy Union Causing Unintended Access on anihpj

The Problem: You have two CNPs in anihpj — one restricting access and one for observability. Combined, they allow unintended access because Cilium uses policy union (OR logic). A pod that should be blocked can reach the API.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600
kubectl create deployment monitor -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600

kubectl apply -f - << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: web}}]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]}]
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-monitoring
  namespace: anihpj              # ❌ BUG: Second CNP adds OR logic — monitor can also reach API!
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: monitor}}]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]}]
CNP
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Both CNPs applied: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj → restrict-api, allow-monitoring ✅
✓2. Web→api works (expected): kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget http://api-ip:80 → HTTP 200 ✅
✗3. Monitor→api WORKS (unexpected!): kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/monitor -- wget http://api-ip:80 → HTTP 200! ❌
✗4. Policy union effect: Two CNPs combine with OR — allow-monitoring grants access monitor doesn't need ❌
✗5. Expected only web→api allowed, but monitor also has access due to second CNP ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List all CNPs: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj
→ Two CNPs: restrict-api + allow-monitoring — both target app=api endpoints
2Check allow-monitoring rules: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj allow-monitoring -o yaml | grep -A5 fromEndpoints
→ Allows fromEndpoints: {app: monitor} — monitor can reach API!
3Understand policy union: Multiple CNPs targeting the same endpoint combine with OR logic — any policy can grant access
4Expected behavior: restrict-api should be the ONLY policy governing API access — allow-monitoring accidentally widens access
5Root cause identified: Two CNPs on same endpoint combine via OR logic — allow-monitoring unintentionally grants access to monitor pods
🔧

🔧 Fix — Remove or Restrict the Overly Permissive Second CNP

BASH
kubectl delete cnp -n anihpj allow-monitoring
# If monitoring access is needed, restrict it to specific monitoring functions, not full HTTP access
✓

✅ Verify — Only Web Pods Can Reach API

After removing the allow-monitoring CNP, only web pods can reach the API. Monitor pods are now DROPPED. Policy union is a common pitfall when multiple teams manage CNPs independently.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Two CNPs → combined access
②
Policy union = OR logic
③
Second CNP grants extra access
④
Remove permissive CNP
⑤
Only intended access remains

Tenet: Cilium combines multiple CNPs targeting the same endpoint with OR logic (policy union). Any CNP can grant access, even if another CNP is restrictive. Audit all policies on an endpoint with kubectl get cnp -l 'app=api'.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/monitor -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://10.0.1.20:80 HTTP 200 OK ← Monitor should NOT have API access!
$ kubectl get cnp -n anihpj NAME AGE restrict-api 10m allow-monitoring 10m ← Two CNPs on same endpoint
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --from-label app=monitor --to-label app=api --verdict FORWARDED TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION VERDICT 12:01:01 monitor-xxx api-xxx FORWARDED ← Policy union allows it
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://10.0.1.20:80 HTTP 200 OK ✅ Web still allowed
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/monitor -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://10.0.1.20:80 wget: download timed out ✅ Monitor now blocked
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --from-label app=monitor --to-label app=api --verdict DROPPED TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION VERDICT 12:05:01 monitor-xxx api-xxx DROPPED ✅

metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: anihpj-staging
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {}}     # ❌ BUG: No ingress/egress rules = no enforcement!
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnbug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Namespace created: kubectl get ns anihpj-staging → Active ✅
✓2. CNP applied: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj-staging → deny-all ✅
✗3. Pods still communicate: kubectl exec -n anihpj-staging deploy/web -- wget http://api-ip:80 → HTTP 200! ❌
✗4. Hubble shows FORWARDED: hubble observe -n anihpj-staging --verdict FORWARDED → traffic flowing ❌
✗5. CNP has no ingress/egress: empty selector without rules = no enforcement ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check CNP rules: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj-staging deny-all -o yaml
→ No ingress/egress rules — silent allow-all!
2Understand deny-all: A true deny-all needs explicit ingress: [] and egress: []
→ Empty lists = implicit deny; no rules = no enforcement
3Current behavior: endpointSelector: {} without rules = policy exists but does nothing
4Hubble confirms: hubble observe -n anihpj-staging → All traffic FORWARDED, zero policy enforcement
5Root cause identified: CNP has no ingress/egress rules — must explicitly set ingress:[] and egress:[] for deny-all
🔧

🔧 Fix — Add Explicit Empty ingress:[] and egress:[] for True Deny-All

BASH
kubectl delete cnp -n anihpj-staging deny-all
kubectl apply -f - << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: anihpj-staging
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingress: []
  egress: []
CNP
✓

✅ Verify — All Pod Traffic Blocked in Staging

After setting ingress: [] and egress: [], all pod traffic in staging is DROPPED. Hubble shows universal DROPPED verdicts. This is the correct deny-all posture for a locked-down staging environment.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Deny-all not working
②
CNP has no rules = allow
③
Need explicit ingress:[]
④
Add egress:[] too
⑤
All traffic now blocked

Tenet: A true namespace-level deny-all requires explicit ingress: [] and egress: []. A CNP with only an endpointSelector but no rules does nothing — Cilium only enforces when rules are defined.

$ kubectl get cnp -n anihpj-staging deny-all -o yaml | grep -c 'ingress:' 1 ← Has key but empty rules — no enforcement

Fix CCNP Applied to Wrong Nodes — nodeSelector Mismatch

The Problem: You applied a CCNP to secure worker nodes, but the policy is applied to control-plane nodes instead. Worker nodes are unprotected. The nodeSelector is wrong.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine

cat > ccnp-bug.yaml << 'CCNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: worker-firewall
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ""      # ❌ BUG: Targets control-plane, not workers!
  ingress:
  - fromEntities: [cluster]
CCNP
kubectl apply -f ccnp-bug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. CCNP applied: kubectl get ccnp → worker-firewall exists ✅
✓2. Policy active somewhere: cilium policy get → worker-firewall listed ✅
✗3. Worker nodes unprotected: check worker node → no host policy enforced! ❌
✗4. Control-plane nodes have policy: kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep control-plane → matches ❌
✗5. Wrong nodeSelector label: kubectl get ccnp -o yaml | grep nodeSelector → control-plane, not worker! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check CCNP nodeSelector: kubectl get ccnp worker-firewall -o yaml | grep -A3 nodeSelector
→ node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: "" — targets control-plane!
2Check worker node labels: kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/worker
→ Worker nodes have different label: node-role.kubernetes.io/worker
3Verify policy enforcement: cilium endpoint list → Host endpoints on control-plane have policy, workers don't
4Intended target: Policy named "worker-firewall" but selects control-plane — nodeSelector label doesn't match worker nodes
5Root cause identified: CCNP nodeSelector targets control-plane nodes — should target worker nodes with correct label
🔧

🔧 Fix — Correct nodeSelector to Target Worker Nodes

BASH
kubectl delete ccnp worker-firewall
kubectl apply -f - << 'CCNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: worker-firewall
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: ""
  ingress:
  - fromEntities: [cluster]
CCNP
✓

✅ Verify — Worker Nodes Now Have Host Firewall

After fixing the nodeSelector to target node-role.kubernetes.io/worker, the CCNP now applies to worker nodes. Control-plane nodes are no longer affected. cilium endpoint list shows host policy on worker endpoints.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Policy exists but wrong target
②
nodeSelector = control-plane
③
Workers have worker label
④
Fix nodeSelector label
⑤
Workers now protected

Tenet: CCNP nodeSelector determines which nodes the host policy applies to. A mismatched label means the policy applies to wrong nodes — or no nodes at all. Always verify node labels with kubectl get nodes --show-labels.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)

$ kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep worker worker-1 Ready ... node-role.kubernetes.io/worker= ← Workers have different label
$ cilium endpoint list | grep -c 'worker-firewall' 0 ← No worker endpoints have this policy
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix

Debug HTTP Header-Based Policy Not Matching on anihpj

The Problem: You created an L7 CNP requiring X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod header. Requests with the correct header are still DROPPED. Hubble shows the header present but policy denies it.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600

cat > cnbug.yaml << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-auth
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: web}}]
    toPorts:
    - ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]
      rules:
        http:
        - headers: ["X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod "]     # ❌ BUG: Trailing space in header value!
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnbug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → web and api Running ✅
✓2. CNP exists: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj → require-auth applied ✅
✗3. Request WITH correct header blocked: curl -H "X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod" http://api-service → 403! ❌
✗4. Hubble shows header present but DROPPED: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json → header "anihpj-prod" but verdict DROPPED ❌
✗5. CNP header value has trailing space: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj -o yaml | grep headers → "anihpj-prod " (note space!) ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Inspect CNP header rule: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj require-auth -o yaml | grep -A2 headers
→ "X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod " — trailing space after "prod"!
2Verify request header: curl -v -H "X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod" http://api-service 2>&1 | grep X-Auth
→ Request sends "anihpj-prod" (no trailing space)
3String mismatch: CNP expects "anihpj-prod " (with space) but request sends "anihpj-prod" — exact string match fails
4Hubble L7 detail: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq '.flow.l7.http.headers' → Header value doesn't match policy
5Root cause identified: Trailing space in CNP header value — "anihpj-prod " ≠ "anihpj-prod" — exact string match fails silently
🔧

🔧 Fix — Remove Trailing Space from Header Value

BASH
kubectl patch cnp -n anihpj require-auth --type json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/ingress/0/toPorts/0/rules/http/0/headers/0","value":"X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod"}]'
✓

✅ Verify — Correct Header Now Matches

After removing the trailing space, requests with X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod return HTTP 200. Wrong tokens still return 403. hubble observe shows FORWARDED for matching headers.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Header present but denied
②
CNP value has trailing space
③
Exact string match fails
④
Remove trailing space
⑤
Header now matches

Tenet: L7 HTTP header rules use exact string matching. A trailing space, extra character, or encoding issue in the CNP YAML silently breaks the match. Always verify header values are trimmed and match exactly.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -H "X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod" http://api-service 403 ← Correct header but policy denies!
$ kubectl get cnp -n anihpj require-auth -o yaml | grep headers - "X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod " ← Note trailing space!
$ hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq '.flow.l7.http.headers[].value, .flow.verdict' "anihpj-prod" "DROPPED" ← Header correct but policy has trailing space
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -H "X-Auth-Token: anihpj-prod" http://api-service 200 ✅ Matching header allowed
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -H "X-Auth-Token: wrong" http://api-service 403 ✅ Wrong token still denied
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict FORWARDED TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION VERDICT 12:08:01 web-xxx api-service FORWARDED ✅

Fix Policy Import/Export Between anihpj Dev and Prod Clusters

The Problem: You exported a CNP from the dev cluster and imported it to prod, but the policy doesn't work in prod. The endpointSelector references labels that don't exist in the prod namespace.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
# In DEV cluster — export the policy
kubectl get cnp -n anihpj allow-api -o yaml > dev-policy.yaml

# In PROD cluster — import and apply
kubectl create namespace anihpj-prod
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj-prod --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj-prod --image=busybox -- sleep 3600

cat dev-policy.yaml
# Shows: endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {tier: backend}}  ← ❌ BUG!
# Prod pods have: app=api, not tier=backend!
kubectl apply -f dev-policy.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. CNP imported: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj-prod → allow-api exists ✅
✓2. Pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj-prod → web and api Running ✅
✗3. Policy not enforcing: kubectl exec -n anihpj-prod deploy/web -- wget http://api-ip:80 → TIMEOUT! ❌ (expected FORWARDED)
✗4. cilium policy selectors: cilium policy selectors -n anihpj-prod → allow-api: 0 endpoints ❌
✗5. Label mismatch: dev uses "tier: backend", prod uses "app: api" ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check CNP selector: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj-prod allow-api -o yaml | grep -A3 endpointSelector
→ matchLabels: {tier: backend} — dev labels, not prod!
2Check prod pod labels: kubectl get pods -n anihpj-prod --show-labels | grep api
→ app=api — prod uses different labeling convention
3Policy import gap: Direct YAML export/import doesn't transform labels between environments
4Zero endpoints selected: cilium policy selectors -n anihpj-prod → 0 endpoints matched
5Root cause identified: Exported CNP uses dev labels (tier: backend) — prod pods use different labels (app: api)
🔧

🔧 Fix — Update endpointSelector Labels for Prod Environment

BASH
kubectl patch cnp -n anihpj-prod allow-api --type merge -p '{"spec":{"endpointSelector":{"matchLabels":{"app":"api"}}}}'
✓

✅ Verify — Policy Enforces in Prod with Correct Labels

After updating the endpointSelector to match prod labels (app: api), the CNP now selects the API pods. Traffic from web to api is FORWARDED. Always review and adapt imported policies for each environment.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Policy imported but broken
②
Dev labels ≠ prod labels
③
Selector matches 0 pods
④
Update to prod labels
⑤
Policy now enforces

Tenet: CiliumNetworkPolicy export/import between clusters requires label adaptation. Different environments often use different labeling conventions. Always verify endpointSelector matches target pod labels after import.

$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj-prod --show-labels | grep api api-xxx Running app=api ← Prod uses different labels

$ kubectl exec -n anihpj-prod deploy/web -- wget -qO- http://10.0.1.20:80 HTTP 200 OK ✅ Policy works in prod

S38
🧪 SCENARIO S38 — Category 2: Network Policy

Fix L7 Policy Bypass via Alternative HTTP Method on anihpj

The Problem: Your CNP blocks POST /admin but attackers use PUT /admin instead and it works. The L7 rule only blocks POST, but PUT and DELETE are allowed. You need to lock down ALL write methods.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600

cat > cnbug.yaml << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-post-admin
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: web}}]
    toPorts:
    - ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]
      rules:
        http:
        - method: POST            # ❌ BUG: Only blocks POST — PUT/DELETE bypass!
          path: "^/admin"
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnbug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → web and api Running ✅
✓2. POST /admin blocked: curl -X POST http://api-service/admin → 403! ✅
✗3. PUT /admin WORKS (bypass!): curl -X PUT http://api-service/admin → HTTP 200! ❌
✗4. DELETE /admin WORKS: curl -X DELETE http://api-service/admin → HTTP 200! ❌
✗5. Hubble shows PUT FORWARDED: hubble observe -n anihpj --http-method PUT → FORWARDED! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check blocked methods: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj block-post-admin -o yaml | grep method
→ Only POST listed — PUT, DELETE, PATCH are NOT blocked!
2Understand L7 method logic: Cilium L7 HTTP uses allow-list for methods — listing POST as denied means only POST is filtered
3Test alternative methods: PUT, DELETE, PATCH all bypass the POST-only rule
→ Any method not explicitly listed passes through!
4Hubble confirms bypass: hubble observe -n anihpj --http-method PUT --verdict FORWARDED → PUT bypasses the POST-only rule
5Root cause identified: L7 rule only restricts POST — attackers bypass using PUT, DELETE, PATCH, or other HTTP methods
🔧

🔧 Fix — Block ALL Write Methods (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH) on /admin

BASH
kubectl delete cnp -n anihpj block-post-admin
kubectl apply -f - << 'CNP'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-admin-writes
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: web}}]
    toPorts:
    - ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]
      rules:
        http:
        - method: GET
          path: "^/admin"
        - method: POST            # Block write methods on /admin
          path: "^/admin"
        - method: PUT
          path: "^/admin"
        - method: DELETE
          path: "^/admin"
CNP
✓

✅ Verify — All Write Methods Blocked, GET Allowed

After adding explicit blocks for POST, PUT, and DELETE on /admin, all write methods return 403. GET /admin still returns 200. hubble observe shows DROPPED for all blocked methods.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
POST blocked but PUT works
②
Only POST in rule
③
PUT/DELETE bypass
④
Add all write methods
⑤
Full coverage achieved

Tenet: L7 HTTP method rules in Cilium use explicit listing. Blocking only POST leaves PUT, DELETE, PATCH, and other methods unrestricted. For comprehensive protection, list ALL methods you want to control — both allowed and denied.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X PUT http://api-service/admin 200 ← PUT bypasses POST-only rule!
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X DELETE http://api-service/admin 200 ← DELETE also bypasses!
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --http-method PUT --verdict FORWARDED TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION HTTP VERDICT 12:01:01 web-xxx api-service PUT /admin FORWARDED ← Bypass!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X PUT http://api-service/admin 403 ✅ PUT now blocked
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X DELETE http://api-service/admin 403 ✅ DELETE now blocked
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://api-service/admin 200 ✅ GET /admin still allowed
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --http-method PUT --verdict DROPPED TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION HTTP VERDICT 12:05:01 web-xxx api-service PUT /admin DROPPED ✅
🧹

The Problem: Cilium is installed with kube-proxy replacement in partial mode. You need strict mode for full eBPF-based load balancing, but after enabling it, anihpj services stop working. KPR strict mode requires additional configuration.

cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement
# → KubeProxyReplacement: Partial

# ❌ BUG: Switching to strict without enabling socket-LB and nodePort acceleration
cilium config set kube-proxy-replacement strict
kubectl rollout restart daemonset cilium -n kube-system

kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. KPR mode changed: cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement → Strict ✅
✓2. Pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → 3 api pods Running ✅
✗3. Service unreachable: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl --connect-timeout 3 http://api-service → TIMEOUT! ❌
✗4. cilium service list shows no backends: cilium service list → api-service has 0 backends! ❌
✗5. Socket-level LB not enabled: cilium config | grep socket-lb → disabled ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check KPR mode: cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement
→ Strict — but strict mode requires socket-LB for connect() interception!
2Check socket-LB status: cilium config | grep -i socket
→ socket-lb-hostns-only: false — socket-level load balancing NOT enabled
3Check service backends: cilium service list
→ api-service: Frontend=10.96.x.x, Backends=0 — no backends populated!
4Understand KPR modes: Partial=services handled by kube-proxy; Strict=Cilium handles ALL services via eBPF — needs socket-LB
5Root cause identified: KPR strict mode enabled without socket-LB — pod-to-service connect() calls not intercepted by eBPF
🔧

🔧 Fix — Enable Socket-Level Load Balancing for KPR Strict Mode

BASH
cilium config set socket-lb-hostns-only false
cilium config set bpf-lb-sock true
kubectl rollout restart daemonset cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status daemonset cilium -n kube-system --timeout=120s
✓

✅ Verify — Service Load Balancing Works via eBPF

After enabling socket-LB, cilium service list shows 3 backends for api-service. curl http://api-service returns HTTP 200 with Maglev-based load balancing across all 3 api pods.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
KPR strict enabled → services break
②
Socket-LB not enabled
③
0 backends in cilium service list
④
Enable socket-LB + bpf-lb-sock
⑤
Services work via eBPF

Tenet: KPR strict mode replaces kube-proxy entirely with eBPF-based load balancing. It requires socket-LB (connect() interception at socket level) and bpf-lb-sock. Without these, pod-to-service traffic bypasses Cilium's eBPF datapath.

$ cilium config | grep -i socket socket-lb-hostns-only false ← Not enabled

$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://api-service 200 ✅ Service reachable via eBPF load balancing

Debug Maglev Hashing Causing Uneven Backend Distribution on anihpj

The Problem: KPR strict mode is enabled with Maglev hashing, but one api pod receives 80% of traffic while the other two get 10% each. Maglev should provide consistent, even distribution. The lookup table is incorrectly sized.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: Maglev table size too small for 3 backends
cilium config set maglev-table-size 7    # Should be a prime number near expected backends * 100
kubectl rollout restart daemonset cilium -n kube-system
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Service created: kubectl get svc -n anihpj → api-service ✅
✓2. All 3 pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → 3/3 Ready ✅
✗3. Uneven load: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- sh -c "for i in $(seq 100); do curl -s http://api-service 2>&1 | grep server_name; done" | sort | uniq -c → 80/10/10 split! ❌
✗4. Maglev table too small: cilium config | grep maglev → table-size=7 (prime but tiny!) ❌
✗5. cilium service list shows skewed backend weights: table-size=7 cannot evenly distribute 3 backends ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Maglev table size: cilium config | grep maglev
→ maglev-table-size: 7 — M (table size) must be prime and >> N (backends)!
2Understand Maglev hashing: Maglev uses a lookup table of size M (prime). With M=7 and N=3 backends, slots distribute unevenly: backend1 gets 3 slots, others 2 each
→ Uneven distribution: 43%/28%/28%
3Recommended sizing: M should be a prime number ~100x the maximum expected backends — for 10 backends, use M=1009 or M=1637
4Check actual distribution: Run multiple requests and count which backend responds — confirms uneven split
5Root cause identified: Maglev table size (M=7) too small — needs prime M >> N backends for even distribution
🔧

🔧 Fix — Increase Maglev Table Size to a Large Prime Number

BASH
cilium config set maglev-table-size 16381
kubectl rollout restart daemonset cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status daemonset cilium -n kube-system --timeout=120s
✓

✅ Verify — Even Traffic Distribution Across All Backends

After setting maglev-table-size=16381, traffic distributes evenly across all 3 backends (~33% each). Maglev's consistent hashing now works correctly with a properly sized lookup table.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Uneven load distribution
②
Maglev table size = 7
③
M too small for N=3
④
Set M to large prime (16381)
⑤
Even ~33% distribution

Tenet: Maglev hashing uses a lookup table of size M (must be prime). For even distribution, M should be much larger than the number of backends N — typically M ≈ N × 100. Common values: 16381, 65537. A small M causes skewed slot assignment.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ cilium config | grep maglev maglev-table-size 7 ← Tiny! 3 backends, 7 slots
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- sh -c "for i in $(seq 30); do curl -s http://api-service | grep -o 'server_[0-9]'; done" | sort | uniq -c 24 server_1 3 server_2 3 server_3 ← Highly skewed!
$ cilium service list ID Frontend Backends 1 10.96.100.50:80 10.0.1.10:80(13),10.0.2.11:80(3),10.0.1.12:80(3) ← 13 vs 3 slots
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cilium config | grep maglev maglev-table-size 16381 ✅ Large prime
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- sh -c "for i in $(seq 30); do curl -s http://api-service | grep -o 'server_[0-9]'; done" | sort | uniq -c 10 server_1 10 server_2 10 server_3 ✅ Even distribution

NodePort unreachable

KPR strict mode

bpf-lb-acceleration disabled

Enable acceleration=native

1Check Ingress TLS config: kubectl get ingress -n anihpj anihpj-ingress -o yaml | grep secretName

①
HTTPS fails, HTTP works
②
TLS secret exists
③
secretName mismatch
④
Fix secret name
⑤
HTTPS works

Tenet: Cilium Ingress uses secretName from the Ingress TLS spec. The name must exactly match the Kubernetes Secret name. A typo silently prevents TLS from working — the Ingress appears to exist but HTTPS fails.

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix

Debug Ingress Routing to Wrong anihpj Backend

The Problem: You configured Cilium Ingress with two paths: /api → api-service and / → web-service. But all requests go to web-service, even /api requests. The path routing isn't working.

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine

kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

metadata:
  name: anihpj-routes
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Exact                # ❌ BUG: Exact match — /api/health won't match!
        backend:
          service:

      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Ingress created: kubectl get ingress -n anihpj → anihpj-routes ✅
✓2. Both services exist: kubectl get svc -n anihpj → web and api ✅
✓3. / path works → web: curl http://anihpj.example.com/ → web response ✅
✗4. /api goes to web (WRONG!): curl http://anihpj.example.com/api → web response! ❌
✗5. /api/health goes to web: curl http://anihpj.example.com/api/health → web, not api! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Ingress rules: kubectl get ingress -n anihpj anihpj-routes -o yaml | grep -A5 path
→ /api has pathType: Exact — only matches exactly "/api", NOT "/api/" or "/api/health"!
2Understand pathType: Exact = only the exact path; Prefix = path and all sub-paths
→ /api with Exact type won't match /api/health or /api/ — falls through to / Prefix rule
3Request routing: /api doesn't match Exact (trailing info?), falls to / Prefix → web-service
4Check Cilium Ingress logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=cilium-ingress → shows path mismatch
5Root cause identified: pathType: Exact on /api prevents matching sub-paths — /api/health falls through to / Prefix rule

🔧 Fix — Change /api pathType from Exact to Prefix

BASH
kubectl patch ingress -n anihpj anihpj-routes --type json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/http/paths/0/pathType","value":"Prefix"}]'

After changing pathType to Prefix, /api, /api/health, and /api/v1/jobs all route to the api-service. The web service handles / and other paths.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
All paths → web
②
/api pathType = Exact
③
Exact = no sub-paths
④
Change to Prefix
⑤
/api routes correctly

Tenet: pathType: Exact matches only the exact path with no sub-path matching. pathType: Prefix matches the path and all paths under it. Always use Prefix for API routes that have sub-resources.

✓1. Ingress with retry: kubectl get ingress -n anihpj → retry=3 ✅
✓2. GET requests retry correctly: curl http://anihpj/api/jobs → returns even on transient failure ✅
✗3. POST duplicated: simulated slow POST → 2 job postings created instead of 1! ❌
✗4. Retry applies to all methods: kubectl get ingress -n anihpj -o yaml | grep retry → no method restriction ❌
✗5. No idempotency on POST: retrying non-idempotent methods causes side effects ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check retry config: kubectl get ingress -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 retry
→ retry=3 on ALL methods — POST, PUT, DELETE all retry!
2Understand retry safety: GET/HEAD are idempotent (safe to retry); POST/PUT/DELETE are NOT
→ Retrying a POST creates duplicate resources
3Check for method-specific retry: Cilium Ingress supports ingress.cilium.io/retry-on-methods to restrict retry to safe methods
4Impact on jobpost: Each POST /api/jobs creates a new job listing — retry creates duplicates that confuse users
5Root cause identified: Retry policy applies to ALL HTTP methods including non-idempotent POST — duplicates job submissions
🔧

🔧 Fix — Restrict Retries to Idempotent Methods (GET, HEAD) Only

BASH
kubectl annotate ingress -n anihpj anihpj-ingress \
  ingress.cilium.io/retry-on-methods="GET,HEAD" --overwrite
✓

✅ Verify — GET Retries Work, POST Never Retried

After restricting retries to GET,HEAD only, transient GET failures are retried while POST never retries. No more duplicate job submissions. Safe retry configuration for anihpj.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Duplicate POST submissions
②
Retry on all methods
③
POST is non-idempotent
④
Restrict to GET/HEAD
⑤
No duplicates

Tenet: Retry policies on non-idempotent HTTP methods (POST, PUT, DELETE) cause side effects like duplicate resource creation. Always restrict retries to safe methods using retry-on-methods: GET,HEAD. Never retry POST on write APIs.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -X POST -d 'title=test' --connect-timeout 2 http://anihpj/api/jobs HTTP 201 Created ... (first attempt) ... HTTP 201 Created ... (retry!) ... ← Duplicate!
$ kubectl get ingress -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 retry ingress.cilium.io/retry: 3 ingress.cilium.io/retry-timeout: 500ms ← No method restriction
$ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj | wc -l 3 ← 1 POST created 2 jobs via retry
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -X POST -d 'title=test2' --connect-timeout 2 http://anihpj/api/jobs HTTP 201 Created ✅ Single creation, no retry
$ kubectl annotate ingress -n anihpj anihpj-ingress ingress.cilium.io/retry-on-methods --overwrite GET,HEAD ✅ Only safe methods retried
$ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj | wc -l 2 ✅ One new job, no duplicate
🧹

🧹 Cleanup

BASH
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

kubectl rollout status daemonset cilium -n kube-system --timeout=120s

①
Bandwidth not limited
②
EDT requires kernel 5.18+
③
Current kernel too old
④
Enable legacy TBF mode
⑤
50Mbps cap enforced

Tenet: Cilium Bandwidth Manager uses EDT (Earliest Departure Time) for optimal rate limiting — requires kernel 5.18+. For older kernels, enable bandwidth-manager-legacy for TBF-based limiting. Always check cilium status after enabling.

$ uname -r 5.15.0-generic ← Needs 5.18+ for EDT

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix

$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -O /dev/null http://fileserver/1GB 2>&1 | grep -o '[0-9.]* MB/s' 6.2 MB/s ✅ ~50Mbps enforced

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BBR enabled but not active
②
Bandwidth Manager disabled
③
BBR is a BW Manager feature
④
Enable both together

BBR now active

$ cilium config | grep bandwidth-manager enable-bandwidth-manager true ✅ Both enabled

The Problem: You annotated a running anihpj pod with bandwidth limits, but the limits are not enforced. Only newly created pods get the limits. Restarting the pod would cause downtime.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH

# ❌ BUG: Annotating RUNNING pod — annotation not picked up without restart

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Bandwidth Manager enabled: cilium status | grep Bandwidth → OK ✅
✓2. Annotation added: kubectl get pod -n anihpj $POD -o yaml | grep bandwidth → 50M ✅
✗3. Bandwidth NOT enforced on annotated pod: wget from annotated pod → full speed! ❌
✗4. New pods work: create a new pod with the annotation → bandwidth enforced ✅

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Cilium endpoint: cilium endpoint get

5Root cause identified: Bandwidth annotations are only read at pod creation — annotating a running pod has no effect without restart

①
Annotation on running pod ignored
②
Cilium reads at pod creation
③
No dynamic update
④
Rollout restart needed
⑤
New pods get limits

Tenet: Bandwidth annotations (kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth) are only read by Cilium at pod creation time. Annotating a running pod has no effect. Use kubectl rollout restart or update the Deployment template to apply changes.

The Problem: You want mutual TLS between web and api without service mesh sidecars. Cilium supports sidecar-free mTLS, but traffic between web and api is unencrypted. Hubble shows plain HTTP, not TLS.

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=busybox -- sleep 3600

# ❌ BUG: Mutual auth enabled but no TLS secret or policy configured

kubectl rollout restart daemonset cilium -n kube-system

# Missing: CiliumNetworkPolicy with authentication mode "required"

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-web-to-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: web}}]
      # ❌ BUG: No authentication mode specified!
CNP
kubectl apply -f cnp-bug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Mutual auth enabled: cilium config | grep mutual-auth → true ✅
✓2. CNP allows web→api: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj → allow-web-to-api ✅
✗3. Traffic unencrypted: hubble observe -n anihpj --from-label app=web → plain HTTP, no TLS! ❌
✗4. No authentication in CNP: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj -o yaml | grep authentication → not found! ❌
✗5. Hubble shows no TLS: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq .flow.is_reply.TLS → null ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check CNP authentication: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj allow-web-to-api -o yaml | grep -A3 authentication
→ No authentication field — mTLS not enforced!
2Understand sidecar-free mTLS: Requires: enable-mutual-auth=true + CNP with authentication.mode: required
3Check mutual auth status: cilium status | grep -i mutual
→ Mutual Authentication: Enabled — but no policy requires it
4Required CNP structure: Add authentication: {mode: required} to the ingress rule to enforce mTLS
5Root cause identified: Mutual auth globally enabled but CNP missing authentication.mode: required — mTLS not enforced
🔧

🔧 Fix — Add authentication.mode: required to CNP for mTLS

BASH
kubectl patch cnp -n anihpj allow-web-to-api --type merge -p '{"spec":{"ingress":[{"fromEndpoints":[{"matchLabels":{"app":"web"}}],"authentication":{"mode":"required"}}]}}'

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Traffic unencrypted
②
Mutual auth globally enabled
③
CNP lacks auth mode
④
Add mode:required
⑤
mTLS enforced

Tenet: Cilium sidecar-free mTLS requires two things: enable-mutual-auth=true (global) AND authentication.mode: required in the CNP ingress rule. Without the CNP-level setting, mutual auth is available but not enforced.

✅ Verify — HTTPRoute Accepted, Requests Return 200

After aligning the Gateway listener port to 80, the HTTPRoute is accepted. curl http://anihpj.example.com returns HTTP 200 via the web backend. Gateway API routes traffic correctly.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
404 on all requests
②
Gateway port = 8080
③
Route expects port 80
④
Port mismatch
⑤
Align ports → 200 OK

Tenet: Gateway API HTTPRoute.parentRefs.port must match the Gateway.listeners.port. A port mismatch causes the route to not be accepted — resulting in 404 for all requests. Always verify listener and route ports align.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s http://anihpj.example.com 404 Not Found ← Route not attached to gateway
$ kubectl get gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep port port: 8080 ← Gateway listens on 8080
$ kubectl get httproute -n anihpj -o yaml | grep port port: 80 ← Route references port 80 — mismatch!
$ kubectl describe httproute -n anihpj anihpj-route | grep -A2 Status Status: Parents: Message: No listeners match this route
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://anihpj.example.com 200 ✅ Route attached, traffic flowing
$ kubectl describe httproute -n anihpj anihpj-route | grep -A2 Status Status: Parents: Message: Route accepted ✅

Resolve externalTrafficPolicy Local vs Cluster Behavior on anihpj

The Problem: You set externalTrafficPolicy: Local on an anihpj NodePort service, but traffic to nodes without local pods is DROPPED. Some external clients get timeouts depending on which node receives the request.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
# Create 3-node cluster — api pod only on node-1
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1
# Pin pod to node-1
kubectl patch deployment api -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"kubernetes.io/hostname":"node-1"}}}}}'

cat > svc-bug.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  type: NodePort
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local      # ❌ BUG: Local drops traffic to nodes without pods!
  selector: {app: api}
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    nodePort: 30080
EOF
kubectl apply -f svc-bug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Service created: kubectl get svc -n anihpj → api-service NodePort:30080 ✅
✓2. Node-1 (has pod) works: curl http://node-1:30080 → HTTP 200 ✅
✗3. Node-2 (no pod) TIMEOUT: curl http://node-2:30080 → TIMEOUT! ❌
✗4. Node-3 (no pod) TIMEOUT: curl http://node-3:30080 → TIMEOUT! ❌
✗5. 66% of external requests fail: only 1 of 3 nodes has the pod ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod placement: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
→ api pod only on node-1 — nodes 2 and 3 have no local pod
2Understand externalTrafficPolicy: Local = only forward to pods on the receiving node; Cluster = forward to any pod across nodes
→ Local drops traffic on nodes without local pods — no cross-node forwarding!
3Check service config: kubectl get svc -n anihpj -o yaml | grep externalTrafficPolicy
→ Local — problematic with single pod
4Use case mismatch: Local preserves source IP but only works when every node has a pod — not suitable for single-replica services
5Root cause identified: externalTrafficPolicy: Local with single pod on one node — nodes without local pods drop traffic
🔧

🔧 Fix — Change externalTrafficPolicy to Cluster or Scale Pods

BASH
kubectl patch svc -n anihpj api-service -p '{"spec":{"externalTrafficPolicy":"Cluster"}}'
# OR: Scale to 3 replicas so every node has a pod
# kubectl scale deployment api -n anihpj --replicas=3
✓

✅ Verify — All Nodes Respond to NodePort Requests

After switching to externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster, all three nodes respond to NodePort requests. Traffic arriving at node-2/3 is forwarded to node-1's pod. External clients no longer see timeouts.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
NodePort timeout on 2/3 nodes
②
externalTrafficPolicy=Local
③
Pod only on node-1
④
Local = no cross-node
⑤
Switch to Cluster → all work

Tenet: externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves the client source IP but only forwards to pods on the receiving node. Nodes without local pods drop traffic. Use Cluster for services with uneven pod distribution or when source IP preservation isn't critical.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl --connect-timeout 3 http://node-2:30080 curl: (28) Connection timed out ← Node without pod
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide NAME NODE api-xxx node-1 ← Only on node-1!
$ kubectl get svc -n anihpj -o yaml | grep externalTrafficPolicy externalTrafficPolicy: Local ← Drops traffic on nodes without local pods
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s http://node-1:30080 | head -1 HTTP/1.1 200 OK ✅ Node-1 works
$ curl -s http://node-2:30080 | head -1 HTTP/1.1 200 OK ✅ Node-2 now forwards to node-1
$ curl -s http://node-3:30080 | head -1 HTTP/1.1 200 OK ✅ All nodes respond

🧪 SCENARIO S53 — Category 3: Service Mesh

Debug DSR Causing Asymmetric Routing for anihpj

The Problem: You enabled DSR (Direct Server Return) on anihpj services, but some clients see connection resets. Traffic paths are asymmetric — requests go through one node, responses come directly from pod to client, bypassing the original node.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: DSR enabled but client network doesn't allow direct pod-to-client responses
cilium config set enable-dsr true
kubectl rollout restart daemonset cilium -n kube-system
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. DSR enabled: cilium config | grep dsr → true ✅
✓2. Service works from some clients: internal cluster clients OK ✅
✗3. External clients get resets: curl http://api-service from external → Connection reset! ❌
✗4. Asymmetric path: Request goes node→pod, response goes pod→client directly (bypasses node) ❌
✗5. Client firewall blocks: direct pod-to-client response dropped because source IP is pod IP, not node IP ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check DSR status: cilium config | grep dsr
→ enable-dsr: true — DSR active
2Understand DSR flow: With DSR, the response goes directly from pod to client, bypassing the node
→ Response source IP = pod IP (not node IP) — client firewall may reject!
3Check asymmetric path: hubble observe -n anihpj --from-label app=api -o json | jq '.flow.IP.source, .flow.IP.destination'
→ Response goes to external client IP directly from pod
4Client-side firewall: Stateful firewalls expect response from the same IP they sent to (node IP) — DSR breaks this assumption
5Root cause identified: DSR causes asymmetric routing — responses come from pod IP, not node IP, and client firewalls reject them
🔧

🔧 Fix — Disable DSR for Clients Behind Stateful Firewalls

BASH
cilium config set enable-dsr false
kubectl rollout restart daemonset cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status daemonset cilium -n kube-system --timeout=120s
✓

✅ Verify — Symmetric Routing Restored, All Clients Work

After disabling DSR, responses follow the symmetric path (client→node→pod→node→client). curl from external clients returns HTTP 200 because responses come from the expected node IP.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
External clients get resets
②
DSR enabled
③
Asymmetric response path
④
Client firewall rejects pod IP
⑤
Disable DSR → symmetric

Tenet: DSR (Direct Server Return) sends responses directly from pod to client, improving throughput but creating asymmetric paths. This breaks stateful firewalls and NAT that expect responses from the original destination IP. Disable DSR if clients are behind firewalls.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl --connect-timeout 3 http://api-service:30080 curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer ← Asymmetric response rejected
$ cilium config | grep dsr enable-dsr true ← Asymmetric routing active
$ hubble observe -n anihpj --from-label app=api -o json | jq '.flow.IP' "source": "10.0.1.10" (pod IP) "destination": "203.0.113.50" (client) ← Direct pod→client!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://api-service:30080 200 ✅ Symmetric routing works for all clients
$ cilium config | grep dsr enable-dsr false ✅ Symmetric path restored
🧹

🧹 Cleanup

BASH
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

Fix Session Affinity (Sticky Sessions) for anihpj Stateful Endpoints

The Problem: anihpj has a stateful endpoint that requires sticky sessions. You enabled session affinity, but requests still rotate across backends. The session affinity cookie is not being set or honored.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

cat > svc-bug.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector: {app: api}
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP           # ❌ BUG: ClientIP uses source IP — same IP behind NAT = same backend!
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
kubectl apply -f svc-bug.yaml
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✓1. Service with session affinity: kubectl get svc -n anihpj → sessionAffinity: ClientIP ✅
✓2. Pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → 3 api pods ✅
✗3. Requests rotate: for i in $(seq 10); do curl -s http://api-service | grep server_name; done → different backends! ❌
✗4. ClientIP affinity broken behind NAT: all clients appear as same source IP → all get same backend ❌
✗5. No cookie-based affinity: Kubernetes ClientIP uses source IP hash — unreliable behind NAT/LB ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check session affinity type: kubectl get svc -n anihpj -o yaml | grep sessionAffinity
→ ClientIP — uses hash of client source IP
2Understand ClientIP limitation: Behind NAT or load balancer, all clients share the same source IP — ClientIP assigns them ALL to the same backend
→ No real session stickiness for individual users!
3Check Cilium alternatives: Cilium supports sessionAffinity: ClientIP via kube-proxy replacement with Maglev consistent hashing
4For HTTP-based affinity: Cilium Ingress supports cookie-based session affinity — more reliable for web apps behind NAT
5Root cause identified: ClientIP session affinity uses source IP hash — all clients behind same NAT get the same backend, defeating stickiness
🔧

🔧 Fix — Use Cilium Cookie-Based Session Affinity for HTTP Apps

BASH
kubectl annotate svc -n anihpj api-service \
  service.cilium.io/session-affinity=true \
  service.cilium.io/session-affinity-cookie-name=ANIH PJ_SESSION --overwrite
# For Cilium Ingress cookie-based affinity:
kubectl annotate ingress -n anihpj anihpj-ingress \
  ingress.cilium.io/session-affinity=cookie --overwrite
✓

✅ Verify — Requests Stick to Same Backend per Session

After configuring cookie-based session affinity via Cilium, each user session consistently routes to the same backend. curl with the session cookie always hits the same pod. Sticky sessions for anihpj stateful endpoints work correctly.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Requests rotate across backends
②
ClientIP = source IP hash
③
NAT makes all clients same IP
④
Use cookie-based affinity
⑤
Per-session stickiness works

Tenet: sessionAffinity: ClientIP uses source IP hashing — unreliable behind NAT where all clients appear to have the same IP. For HTTP applications, use cookie-based session affinity via Cilium Ingress annotations for true per-user stickiness.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ for i in $(seq 5); do curl -s http://api-service | grep -o "server_[0-9]"; done server_1 server_1 server_1 server_1 server_1 ← All to same backend (ClientIP hash)
$ kubectl get svc -n anihpj -o yaml | grep sessionAffinity sessionAffinity: ClientIP ← Source IP based — broken behind NAT
$ curl -s -b "SESSION=user2" http://api-service | grep -o "server_[0-9]" server_1 ← Different 'user' gets same backend — no real per-user affinity
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -c /tmp/cookie -b /tmp/cookie http://api-service | grep -o "server_[0-9]" server_2 ✅ Session cookie routes to consistent backend
$ curl -s -b /tmp/cookie http://api-service | grep -o "server_[0-9]" server_2 ✅ Same session = same backend
🧹

🧹 Cleanup

BASH
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

Deploy Hubble and Observe anihpj Flows in Real-Time

The Problem: You deployed anihpj but cannot see any network flows. Hubble is installed but not observing traffic for the anihpj namespace. Your job: enable Hubble and observe all anihpj flows in real-time.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Hubble is deployed but flows are empty for anihpj
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80

# Generate traffic
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- http://api:80 2>&1 || true

# Try Hubble — ❌ BUG: no flows!
hubble observe -n anihpj
# (empty output or "no flows")
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble is running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep hubble → Pods are present ✅
✓2. Cilium agent is healthy: cilium status → OK ✅
✗3. Observe anihpj namespace: hubble observe -n anihpj → EMPTY — no flows! ❌
✗4. Observe all namespaces: hubble observe → flows from other namespaces but anihpj missing ❌
✗5. Check Hubble Relay: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/hubble-relay → connection refused to peer service ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Hubble Relay status: kubectl get svc -n kube-system hubble-peer
→ hubble-peer Service has no endpoints — Relay cannot discover peers
2Check Hubble peer service endpoints: kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system hubble-peer
→ — No Cilium agents registered as Hubble peers!
3Check if Hubble is enabled in Cilium: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep -A2 hubble
→ enable-hubble: "false" — Hubble is DISABLED in ConfigMap
4Check Cilium agent Hubble socket: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ls /var/run/cilium/hubble.sock
→ No such file — Hubble socket not created because Hubble is disabled
5Root cause identified: Hubble must be explicitly enabled in Cilium ConfigMap
→ enable-hubble is set to "false" in cilium-config; the Hubble gRPC socket is never created, so Relay cannot aggregate flows
🔧

🔧 Fix — Enable Hubble in ConfigMap

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix: Enable Hubble via Cilium ConfigMap
kubectl patch configmap -n kube-system cilium-config \
  --patch '{"data":{"enable-hubble":"true"}}'

# Restart Cilium agents to pick up the new config
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status ds/cilium -n kube-system

# Restart Hubble Relay
kubectl rollout restart deploy/hubble-relay -n kube-system
kubectl wait --for=condition=available deploy/hubble-relay -n kube-system --timeout=120s

# Verify Hubble peers are registered
kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system hubble-peer
✓

✅ Verify — Hubble Flows Visible for anihpj

After enabling enable-hubble: "true" in the cilium-config ConfigMap and restarting Cilium agents, the hubble-peer Service registers endpoints from each Cilium agent. Hubble Relay connects to all peers and aggregates flows from every node. hubble observe -n anihpj now shows FORWARDED and DROPPED flows with full source/destination pod, verdict, and protocol details.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Deploy anihpj, generate traffic
②
hubble observe -n anihpj → EMPTY
③
Check hubble-peer endpoints → none
④
enable-hubble: "false" in ConfigMap
⑤
Patch ConfigMap → Restart agents

Tenet: Always verify enable-hubble is set to "true" in the cilium-config ConfigMap. Without it, the Hubble gRPC socket is never created on Cilium agents, hubble-peer Service has no endpoints, and Hubble Relay cannot aggregate any flows — resulting in empty hubble observe output.

$ kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep enable-hubble enable-hubble: "false" ← Hubble DISABLED!

$ hubble observe -n anihpj TIMESTAMP SOURCE DESTINATION VERDICT PROTO 12:05:01.123 anihpj/web-xxx:45678 anihpj/api-xxx:80 FORWARDED TCP 12:05:02.456 anihpj/web-yyy:34567 anihpj/api-yyy:80 FORWARDED TCP 12:05:03.789 anihpj/api-xxx:54321 anihpj/anihpj-db:5432 FORWARDED TCP

Debug Hubble Showing No Flows for anihpj Namespace

The Problem: Hubble is enabled and works for other namespaces, but the anihpj namespace shows no flows. Pods are running and communicating, yet Hubble reports zero traffic. Your job: find why Hubble is blind to the anihpj namespace.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Hubble works for default namespace but NOT anihpj
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

# Generate traffic
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- http://api:80 2>&1 || true

# ❌ BUG: No flows for anihpj
hubble observe -n anihpj
# (empty)

# But other namespaces work!
hubble observe -n default
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble enabled: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep enable-hubble → "true" ✅
✓2. Hubble Relay running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep hubble-relay → Running ✅
✗3. Observe anihpj: hubble observe -n anihpj → EMPTY! ❌
✗4. Observe default namespace: hubble observe -n default → flows visible! So Hubble works but blind to anihpj ❌
✗5. Check Cilium endpoints for anihpj: kubectl get cep -n anihpj → No CiliumEndpoints! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if Cilium manages the namespace: kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep cilium
→ No Cilium annotations on namespace — namespace may be excluded from Cilium management
2Check CiliumEndpoint CRDs for anihpj: kubectl get cep -n anihpj
→ No resources found — Cilium is NOT managing endpoints in this namespace
3Check pod labels: kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels
→ Pods are labeled but no io.cilium annotations — Cilium not injecting endpoints
4Verify Cilium is CNI for the node: kubectl get nodes -o yaml | grep -A5 annotations | grep cilium
→ Node has cilium.io annotations — Cilium IS the CNI, but the namespace might be excluded
5Root cause identified: Check namespace label io.cilium/network-policy
→ The anihpj namespace is missing the Cilium namespace label; without it, Cilium does not create CiliumEndpoints or observe flows in that namespace

🔧 Fix — Label Namespace for Cilium Management

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix: Label the namespace so Cilium manages it
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true --overwrite

# Recreate pods so Cilium creates CiliumEndpoints
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj web api
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -n anihpj -l app --timeout=120s

# Verify CiliumEndpoints created
kubectl get cep -n anihpj

✅ Verify — anihpj Flows Visible in Hubble

After labeling the namespace with io.cilium/network-policy=true and restarting pods, Cilium creates CiliumEndpoint CRDs for all anihpj pods. Hubble now observes and reports all flows in the anihpj namespace. kubectl get cep -n anihpj shows endpoints with valid security identities and IP addresses.

①
hubble observe -n anihpj → EMPTY
②
hubble observe -n default → WORKS
③
kubectl get cep -n anihpj → EMPTY
④
Namespace missing io.cilium label
⑤
Label namespace → Restart pods → Flows appear

Tenet: Cilium only manages namespaces that carry its namespace label (typically io.cilium/network-policy or io.cilium/auto-create-endpoints). Without this label, even though Cilium is the CNI and routes pod traffic, it does not create CiliumEndpoint CRDs or observe flows via Hubble for pods in that namespace.
