Filter Hubble Flows — Show Only DROPPED anihpj Traffic

The Problem: You suspect a CiliumNetworkPolicy is dropping traffic for anihpj. Hubble shows all flows (FORWARDED + DROPPED), but you need to filter only DROPPED flows to identify which specific connections are being denied. Your job: use Hubble filters to isolate dropped traffic.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Deploy anihpj with a restrictive CNP (drops api→db)
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true

cat > cnp-restrict.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels: {app: anihpj, tier: db}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels: {app: anihpj, tier: web}
    toPorts:
    - ports: [{port: "5432"}]
EOF
kubectl apply -f cnp-restrict.yaml

kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=web
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=api
kubectl create deployment db -n anihpj --image=postgres:15 -l app=anihpj,tier=db
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl expose deployment db -n anihpj --port=5432

# Generate traffic (some will be dropped)
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/api -- wget -qO- http://db:5432 2>&1 || true

# ❌ BUG: Hubble shows everything — need to isolate DROPPED only
hubble observe -n anihpj
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep hubble-relay → Running ✅
✓2. All flows visible: hubble observe -n anihpj → FORWARDED and DROPPED flows mixed ✅
✗3. Unfiltered output is noisy: hubble observe -n anihpj → hundreds of FORWARDED flows obscuring the DROPPED ones ❌
✗4. No verdict filter used: output includes DNS, HTTP, TCP — need to narrow down to policy drops only ❌
✗5. Cannot tell which exact connection is being denied: need per-flow verdict detail ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Use --verdict flag: hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED
→ Shows only DROPPED flows — api → db:5432 appears as DROPPED
2Add protocol filter: hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED --protocol TCP
→ Further isolates to TCP drops — removes UDP/DNS noise
3Filter by source pod: hubble observe -n anihpj --from-pod anihpj/deploy/api --verdict DROPPED
→ DROPPED flows from api: db port 5432 — CNP is blocking api→db
4Check policy verdict: hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED -o json | jq '.flow.policy_match_type'
→ policy_match_type: 1 — L3/L4 policy denied the connection
5Root cause identified: CNP restrict-db allows only web→db ingress
→ The CNP explicitly allows ingress from tier=web only on port 5432; api (tier=api) is not in the allow list, so its traffic to db is DROPPED
🔧

🔧 Fix — Filter Hubble by Verdict

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Filter Hubble to see only relevant dropped flows
hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED --protocol TCP

# Fix 2: Use JSON output to inspect policy details
hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED -o json | jq '.'

# Fix 3 (if you want to fix the policy, not just observe):
# Add api tier to the allow list in the CNP
kubectl patch cnp restrict-db -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/ingress/0/fromEndpoints/-","value":{"matchLabels":{"app":"anihpj","tier":"api"}}}]'
✓

✅ Verify — DROPPED Flows Isolated and Identified

Using hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --protocol TCP, only denied connections are displayed. The CNP restrict-db is clearly blocking api to db:5432 because only tier=web is in the allow list. JSON output with jq reveals policy_match_type: 1 confirming L3/L4 policy denial.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
hubble observe -n anihpj → mixed FORWARDED+DROPPED
②
--verdict DROPPED → only denied flows
③
--from-pod + --protocol → pinpoint api→db
④
JSON output → policy_match_type confirms L3/L4 deny
⑤
CNP restrict-db allows only web, not api

Tenet: Always use --verdict DROPPED (or --verdict ERROR) to isolate problematic flows. Combine with --from-pod, --to-pod, --protocol, --to-port filters for precision. For deep analysis, -o json with jq exposes policy_match_type, drop_reason_desc, and event_type fields that reveal exactly why each flow was dropped.

The Problem: You need to programmatically analyze anihpj traffic patterns. Hubble's terminal output is human-readable but not machine-parseable. Your job: export flows to JSON and use jq to extract specific insights about anihpj traffic (top talkers, verdict distribution, latency patterns).

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

  kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- http://api:80 2>&1 || true
done

# ❌ BUG: Default text output is hard to parse

# Human-readable but can't filter, count, or aggregate with jq
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble flows visible: hubble observe -n anihpj → FORWARDED flows seen ✅
✓2. Traffic is flowing: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget http://api:80 → 200 OK ✅
✗3. Default output is unstructured: hubble observe -n anihpj | wc -l → hundreds of text lines, cannot count by verdict ❌
✗4. Cannot extract top source pods: text output requires manual parsing, no way to group/count ❌
✗5. Cannot calculate latency percentiles: text output lacks structured latency fields for analysis ❌

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Use JSON output format: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json
→ Each flow becomes a structured JSON object with time, source, destination, verdict, l4, l7, and summary fields
2Extract verdict distribution: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq -r '.flow.verdict' | sort | uniq -c
→ Count of FORWARDED vs DROPPED flows — reveals policy impact
3Find top source pods: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq -r '.flow.source.pod_name' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
→ Identifies which pods generate the most traffic
4Analyze L7 HTTP metrics: hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq '.flow.l7' | jq 'select(. != null)' | jq -r '.http.method + " " + .http.url'
→ Extracts HTTP method, path, and status code from L7 flows
5Root cause identified: Default text output is for human reading only
→ Without -o json, Hubble output cannot be piped to jq for structured analysis; JSON mode unlocks programmatic traffic analysis

🔧 Fix — Export JSON and Analyze with jq

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix: Export to JSON and analyze with jq

# 1. Count flows by verdict
hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq -r '.flow.verdict' | sort | uniq -c

# 2. Top source pods by flow count
hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq -r '.flow.source.pod_name' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10

# 3. Extract HTTP status codes from L7 flows
hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq 'select(.flow.l7.type == "RESPONSE") | .flow.l7.http' | jq -r '[.status, .method, .url] | @tsv'

# 4. Calculate average latency (forward direction)
hubble observe -n anihpj -o json | jq '[.flow.traffic_direction] | length'

# 5. Export to file for offline analysis
hubble observe -n anihpj --last 1000 -o json > anihpj-flows.json
✓

✅ Verify — Structured Flow Analysis with jq

Using hubble observe -o json | jq, flows can be filtered, grouped, and aggregated. Verdict distribution (FORWARDED vs DROPPED), top source pods by flow count, and HTTP method/status breakdown are all available for programmatic analysis. Exported JSON files enable offline analysis and reporting.

②

③

④

⑤
jq selects L7 HTTP fields for method/status analysis

Tenet: Hubble JSON output is the gateway to programmatic observability. Every flow becomes a JSON object with .flow, .node_name, .time, and nested .l4/.l7 fields. Use jq selectors to count verdicts, group by source/destination, filter by protocol, and extract L7 HTTP/Kafka/DNS details. For large datasets, use --last N to limit flows and -o jsonpb for streaming output.

The Problem: You want to visualize anihpj's network traffic using the Hubble UI Service Map. Hubble is enabled but the Hubble UI is not accessible. Your job: deploy the Hubble UI, expose it, and verify the anihpj Service Map shows traffic flows.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Deploy anihpj with traffic
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true

kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=api --replicas=2
kubectl create deployment db -n anihpj --image=postgres:15 -l app=anihpj,tier=db
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl expose deployment db -n anihpj --port=5432

# Generate traffic
for i in $(seq 30); do

  kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/api -- nc -zv db 5432 2>&1 || true
done

# ❌ BUG: Hubble UI not accessible
cilium hubble ui
# Error: Unable to connect or UI not deployed
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble enabled: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep enable-hubble → "true" ✅
✓2. Hubble Relay running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=hubble-relay → Running ✅
✗3. Start Hubble UI: cilium hubble ui → Error: no Hubble UI deployment found ❌
✗4. Check Hubble UI deployment: kubectl get deploy -n kube-system -l k8s-app=hubble-ui → No resources found ❌
✗5. Hubble UI not installed: the UI component is separate from Relay and must be explicitly deployed ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if Hubble UI is deployed: kubectl get all -n kube-system -l k8s-app=hubble-ui
→ No resources — Hubble UI not installed; it is a separate component from Hubble Relay
2Check Helm values for Hubble UI: helm get values cilium -n kube-system | grep -A5 hubble.ui
→ hubble.ui.enabled: false — UI was not enabled during Cilium installation
3Enable Hubble UI via Helm upgrade: helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system --reuse-values --set hubble.ui.enabled=true
→ Helm upgrade adds the Hubble UI Deployment, Service, and RBAC resources
4Alternative: Use cilium CLI to enable: cilium hubble enable --ui
→ The cilium CLI can enable Hubble UI if Hubble was enabled via CLI
5Root cause identified: Hubble UI is an optional component not installed by default
→ Hubble UI must be explicitly enabled via Helm (hubble.ui.enabled=true) or cilium CLI; without it, there is no web frontend for the Service Map
🔧

🔧 Fix — Enable Hubble UI via Helm

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Enable Hubble UI via Helm
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set hubble.ui.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.ui.service.type=ClusterIP

# Wait for Hubble UI to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=available deploy/hubble-ui -n kube-system --timeout=120s

# Fix 2: Access Hubble UI (port-forward)
kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-ui 8081:80 &

# Or use cilium CLI
cilium hubble ui
✓

✅ Verify — Hubble UI Service Map Shows anihpj

After enabling hubble.ui.enabled=true via Helm and deploying the UI, cilium hubble ui opens the Service Map at http://localhost:12000. The dependency graph shows web, api, and db nodes with green (FORWARDED) and red (DROPPED) flow lines. Real-time traffic metrics are visible for all anihpj components.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cilium hubble ui → Error: not deployed
②
kubectl get deploy hubble-ui → not found
③
Helm values: hubble.ui.enabled=false
④
helm upgrade with hubble.ui.enabled=true
⑤
port-forward → Service Map shows anihpj

Tenet: Hubble UI is a separate optional component from Hubble Relay. The Relay aggregates flows; the UI visualizes them. Always verify hubble.ui.enabled=true in Helm values. For production, consider exposing Hubble UI via Cilium Ingress (with auth) instead of port-forward. The Service Map uses color coding: green = FORWARDED, red = DROPPED, yellow = error responses.

Debug Hubble Relay Not Connecting to Peer Service

The Problem: Hubble Relay is deployed but fails to connect to Hubble peers. hubble observe returns 'connection refused' or 'unavailable'. Your job: diagnose why Hubble Relay cannot discover or connect to the Cilium agent Hubble gRPC endpoints.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Deploy anihpj and try to observe
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: Hubble Relay unavailable
hubble observe -n anihpj
# Error: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection error: desc = "transport: Error while dialing: dial tcp: connect: connection refused"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble Relay pod running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=hubble-relay → Running ✅
✓2. Cilium agents running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → All Running ✅
✗3. Try to observe: hubble observe -n anihpj → rpc error: Unavailable, connection refused ❌
✗4. Check Hubble Relay logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/hubble-relay → failed to connect to peer service ❌
✗5. Check peer service: kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system hubble-peer → <none> — No peer endpoints! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Hubble peer service: kubectl describe svc -n kube-system hubble-peer
→ Service exists but has no endpoints — no Cilium agents are registered as Hubble peers
2Check if Hubble is enabled on agents: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium status | grep -i hubble
→ Hubble: Disabled — agents are not running Hubble gRPC server on port 4244
3Verify Hubble socket on agent: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ls -la /var/run/cilium/hubble.sock
→ No such file — Hubble socket was never created because Hubble is disabled
4Check Relay TLS config: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/hubble-relay | grep -i tls
→ TLS handshake error: Hubble Relay expects TLS but agents don't have TLS configured — or vice versa
5Root cause identified: Hubble Relay needs Hubble-enabled agents to connect to via hubble-peer service
→ Either enable-hubble is false on agents (no gRPC server on port 4244) OR TLS configuration mismatch between Relay and agents prevents the connection
🔧

🔧 Fix — Enable Hubble on Cilium Agents

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Enable Hubble on Cilium agents
kubectl patch configmap -n kube-system cilium-config \
  --patch '{"data":{"enable-hubble":"true"}}'

# Fix 2: Restart agents so they start Hubble gRPC server
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status ds/cilium -n kube-system

# Fix 3: Verify peer endpoints register
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.subsets[0].addresses[0].ip}' \
  endpoints/hubble-peer -n kube-system --timeout=120s

# Fix 4: Restart Hubble Relay to connect to new peers
kubectl rollout restart deploy/hubble-relay -n kube-system
kubectl wait --for=condition=available deploy/hubble-relay -n kube-system --timeout=120s

# Fix 5: If TLS mismatch, check certificates
kubectl get secret -n kube-system hubble-relay-client-certs
kubectl get secret -n kube-system hubble-server-certs
✓

✅ Verify — Hubble Relay Connected to All Peers

After enabling Hubble on all Cilium agents and restarting Relay, the hubble-peer Service has endpoints (one per Cilium agent on port 4244). Hubble Relay connects to all peers via gRPC. hubble observe -n anihpj returns aggregated flows from every node in the cluster with FORWARDED/DROPPED verdicts.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
hubble observe → Unavailable / connection refused
②
Hubble Relay logs: failed to connect to peer
③
hubble-peer endpoints →
④
enable-hubble: false in ConfigMap
⑤
Enable Hubble → Restart agents → Restart Relay → Peers register

Tenet: Hubble Relay acts as a multi-node flow aggregator. It discovers Hubble gRPC servers on Cilium agents via the hubble-peer Kubernetes Service (headless, port 4244). Each Cilium agent registers as a peer endpoint when Hubble is enabled. Relay then establishes gRPC streams to all peers and aggregates flows. If any peer is unreachable, Relay logs the error but continues serving from available peers.

Set Up Prometheus to Scrape Hubble Metrics for anihpj

The Problem: You need Prometheus to scrape Hubble metrics for anihpj traffic monitoring. Hubble metrics are enabled but Prometheus cannot scrape them. Your job: configure Hubble metrics and create a ServiceMonitor (or PodMonitor) so Prometheus can collect Hubble's HTTP, DNS, and TCP metrics.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Deploy anihpj and enable Hubble
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=web
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=api
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

# Generate traffic
for i in $(seq 20); do kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- http://api:80 2>&1 || true; done

# ❌ BUG: Prometheus cannot see Hubble metrics
kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-metrics 9965:9965 &
curl -s http://localhost:9965/metrics | head -20
# connection refused — no hubble-metrics service or no metrics endpoint
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble enabled: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep enable-hubble → "true" ✅
✓2. Prometheus running in cluster: kubectl get pods -n monitoring | grep prometheus → Running ✅
✗3. Check Hubble metrics endpoint: curl -s http://localhost:9965/metrics → connection refused — port 9965 not listening ❌
✗4. Check hubble-metrics service: kubectl get svc -n kube-system hubble-metrics → not found ❌
✗5. Prometheus targets: kubectl exec -n monitoring prometheus-xxx -- curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets → no hubble-metrics target ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if Hubble metrics are enabled: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep -A5 hubble-metrics
→ hubble-metrics not configured — metrics server is separate from Hubble flow observability
2Verify metrics port on Cilium agents: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- netstat -tlnp | grep 9965
→ Port 9965 not listening — Cilium agent is not exposing Hubble metrics
3Check Prometheus ServiceMonitor: kubectl get servicemonitor -n kube-system | grep hubble
→ No ServiceMonitor — Prometheus doesn't know to scrape Hubble metrics
4Enable Hubble metrics via Helm: helm get values cilium -n kube-system | grep -A10 hubble.metrics
→ hubble.metrics.enabled is falsy or not set — metrics are opt-in
5Root cause identified: Hubble metrics are a separate opt-in feature requiring explicit configuration
→ Hubble flow observability (enable-hubble) is independent from Hubble metrics (hubble.metrics.enabled). Metrics require: 1) enabling metric types (HTTP, DNS, TCP, etc.), 2) a Service to expose port 9965, and 3) a ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor for Prometheus discovery
🔧

🔧 Fix — Enable Hubble Metrics and ServiceMonitor

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Enable Hubble metrics via Helm
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set hubble.metrics.enabled="{dns,drop,tcp,flow,port-distribution,icmp,http}" \
  --set hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true

# Fix 2: Wait for Cilium agents to restart with metrics
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status ds/cilium -n kube-system

# Fix 3: Verify metrics endpoint
kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-metrics 9965:9965 &
curl -s http://localhost:9965/metrics | grep hubble_http

# Fix 4: Verify Prometheus discovers the target
kubectl get servicemonitor -n kube-system hubble-metrics
✓

✅ Verify — Prometheus Scrapes Hubble Metrics

After enabling hubble.metrics.enabled with HTTP, DNS, TCP, and drop metric types, the hubble-metrics Service exposes port 9965. The ServiceMonitor with release: prometheus label enables Prometheus auto-discovery. Queries for hubble_http_requests_total return request counts by method, path, and status code for anihpj.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
curl localhost:9965/metrics → connection refused
②
hubble-metrics Service not found
③
enable-hubble=true but metrics not enabled
④
Enable hubble.metrics.enabled with metric types
⑤
Create ServiceMonitor → Prometheus discovers target

Tenet: Hubble flow observability (enable-hubble) and Hubble metrics (hubble.metrics.enabled) are separate features. Flows power hubble observe and the UI; metrics power Prometheus/Grafana. Each metric type (HTTP, DNS, TCP, ICMP, drop, flow, port-distribution) adds cardinality — enable only what you need. For anihpj HTTP monitoring, enable http and flow at minimum.

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

# (empty — no Hubble dashboard imported)

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Prometheus scraping metrics: curl -s http://localhost:9965/metrics | grep hubble_http → metrics present ✅
✓2. Grafana running: kubectl get pods -n monitoring -l app=grafana → Running ✅

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Locate Cilium Hubble dashboards: kubectl get cm -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=cilium | grep dashboard
→ Cilium does not deploy dashboards by default — they are available in the Cilium GitHub repo as JSON files

# Hubble DNS Dashboard: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cilium/cilium/main/examples/hubble/hubble-dns-dashboard.json
✓

After importing the Hubble HTTP dashboard as a labeled ConfigMap (grafana_dashboard=1), Grafana auto-discovers it via sidecar provisioning. The dashboard displays anihpj HTTP request rate (QPS), latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), and HTTP status code distribution (200, 404, 500). All panels are powered by Hubble metrics from Prometheus.

The key dashboards are: Hubble HTTP (request rate, latency, status codes), Hubble DNS (query rate, response codes, NXDOMAIN ratio), Hubble TCP (SYN rate, RTT, drops), and Hubble Network Overview (flow rate, drop rate, policy verdicts). Debug Hubble Metrics Not Appearing in Prometheus

The Problem: Hubble metrics are enabled and the endpoint returns data, but Prometheus shows no Hubble metrics. The targets page lists hubble-metrics as 'DOWN' or doesn't list it at all. Your job: find why Prometheus cannot scrape Hubble metrics and fix the discovery/scraping configuration.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Prerequisites: Hubble metrics enabled (from S61)
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=web
kubectl expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: Metrics endpoint works, but Prometheus can't see them
curl -s http://localhost:9965/metrics | head -5
# Returns metrics (endpoint works!)

curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=hubble_http_requests_total
# Empty result — Prometheus has no Hubble data
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble metrics endpoint responds: curl -s http://localhost:9965/metrics | head -5 → 200 OK with metrics ✅
✓2. Prometheus running: kubectl get pods -n monitoring | grep prometheus → Running ✅
✗3. Query Hubble metrics in Prometheus: curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=hubble_http_requests_total' → empty result [] ❌
✗4. Check Prometheus targets: curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets | grep hubble → no hubble target listed ❌
✗5. Prometheus doesn't know about hubble-metrics: ServiceMonitor missing or not matching ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Verify Prometheus discovers hubble-metrics: kubectl get servicemonitor -n kube-system hubble-metrics -o yaml | grep -A10 spec
→ ServiceMonitor exists but matchLabels may not match the hubble-metrics Service
2Check hubble-metrics Service labels: kubectl get svc -n kube-system hubble-metrics -o yaml | grep -A5 labels
→ Service has labels k8s-app: hubble-metrics — verify ServiceMonitor selector matches
3Check Prometheus serviceMonitorSelector: kubectl get prometheus -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -A5 serviceMonitorSelector
→ Prometheus serviceMonitorSelector may filter by a label like release: prometheus that hubble-metrics ServiceMonitor doesn't have
4Verify RBAC for ServiceMonitor: kubectl auth can-i get servicemonitors -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:monitoring:prometheus
→ Prometheus ServiceAccount may lack RBAC to discover ServiceMonitors in kube-system namespace
5Root cause identified: ServiceMonitor selector mismatch or namespace-scoped RBAC
→ Prometheus only discovers ServiceMonitors that match its serviceMonitorSelector AND are in namespaces it's allowed to watch. Common failures: 1) ServiceMonitor missing a required label, 2) Prometheus not watching kube-system namespace, 3) RBAC denying ServiceMonitor read access
🔧

🔧 Fix — Fix ServiceMonitor Label Selector

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Add required label to ServiceMonitor
kubectl label servicemonitor -n kube-system hubble-metrics release=prometheus --overwrite

# Fix 2: Or update Prometheus to watch all namespaces
kubectl patch prometheus -n monitoring prometheus --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"serviceMonitorNamespaceSelector":{"matchLabels":{"kubernetes.io/metadata.name":"kube-system"}}}}'

# Fix 3: Check Prometheus config reloaded
kubectl rollout restart statefulset prometheus -n monitoring
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -n monitoring -l app=prometheus --timeout=120s

# Fix 4: Verify target appears in Prometheus
curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets | jq '.data.activeTargets[] | select(.labels.job == "hubble-metrics")'

# Fix 5: Query Hubble metrics
curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(hubble_http_requests_total[5m])'
✓

✅ Verify — Hubble Metrics Target UP in Prometheus

After adding the release: prometheus label to the hubble-metrics ServiceMonitor and configuring Prometheus to watch the kube-system namespace, the target shows UP in Prometheus. Queries for hubble_http_requests_total, hubble_tcp_flags_total, and hubble_drop_total all return valid anihpj data.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
curl localhost:9965/metrics → OK (endpoint works)
②
Prometheus query → empty (no target)
③
Prometheus targets → no hubble listed
④
ServiceMonitor selector mismatch → missing label
⑤
Add release=prometheus label → Prometheus discovers target

Tenet: When Hubble metrics endpoint returns data but Prometheus can't see them, the issue is almost always a ServiceMonitor selector mismatch. Three things must align: 1) The ServiceMonitor's selector.matchLabels must match the hubble-metrics Service's labels, 2) The ServiceMonitor itself must have labels matching Prometheus's serviceMonitorSelector (commonly release: prometheus), and 3) Prometheus must have RBAC and namespace access to discover ServiceMonitors in that namespace.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)

$ kubectl get servicemonitor -n kube-system hubble-metrics -o yaml | grep -E "release:|matchLabels" labels: k8s-app: hubble-metrics (no "release: prometheus" label) ← Missing required label!
$ kubectl get prometheus -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -A3 serviceMonitorSelector serviceMonitorSelector: matchLabels: release: prometheus ← Prometheus requires this label!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets | jq '.data.activeTargets[] | select(.labels.job=="hubble-metrics") | {health, lastError}' {health: "up", lastError: ""} ✅ Target UP and healthy!
$ curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj"}[5m])' {"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{"method":"GET","status":"200"},"value":[1702,"0.85"]}]}} ✅ anihpj data in Prometheus!

Configure Alert When anihpj HTTP 500 Errors Exceed Threshold

The Problem: anihpj is experiencing intermittent HTTP 500 errors. You have Hubble metrics in Prometheus, but no alerting is configured. Your job: create a PrometheusRule that fires when anihpj's HTTP 500 error rate exceeds 5% of total requests over 5 minutes, and configure Alertmanager to send notifications.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into terminal 
# Deploy anihpj with some failing requests
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=web
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=api
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

# Generate traffic — mix of success and 500 errors
for i in $(seq 100); do kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- wget -qO- http://api:80 2>&1 || true; done

# ❌ BUG: HTTP 500s happening but no alert fires
curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj",status="500"}[5m])'
# Returns non-zero rate but no alert triggered
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Hubble HTTP metrics in Prometheus: curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=hubble_http_requests_total → data present ✅
✓2. Alertmanager running: kubectl get pods -n monitoring | grep alertmanager → Running ✅
✗3. Check Prometheus alerts: curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/rules → no Hubble-related alerting rules defined ❌
✗4. Check PrometheusRules: kubectl get prometheusrule -n monitoring → no anihpj or Hubble rules ❌
✗5. HTTP 500 rate is elevated: rate(hubble_http_requests_total{status="500"}[5m]) → non-zero but no one is notified ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Query current HTTP 500 rate: curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj",status="500"}[5m])'
→ Rate is 0.15/s — if total is 1.0/s, that's 15% — well above 5% threshold
2Query total HTTP rate for comparison: curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj"}[5m])'
→ Total rate is 2.0/s — 500 rate is 7.5% of total traffic
3Check existing PrometheusRules: kubectl get prometheusrule -A
→ No PrometheusRules exist for Hubble metrics — need to create one with the error ratio expression
4Build the alert expression: rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj",status="500"}[5m]) / rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj"}[5m]) > 0.05
→ This PromQL calculates the 500 error ratio over 5 minutes — fires when > 5%
5Root cause identified: PrometheusRule CRD not created for Hubble HTTP error monitoring
→ Hubble metrics are scraped but Prometheus has no alerting rules defined. Alerting requires a PrometheusRule CRD (if using prometheus-operator) or alert rules in prometheus.yml config to evaluate metric expressions and trigger Alertmanager notifications
🔧

🔧 Fix — Create PrometheusRule for HTTP 500 Alert

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Create PrometheusRule for anihpj HTTP 500 errors
cat > hubble-alert-rule.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hubble-http-alerts
  namespace: monitoring
  labels:
    release: prometheus
    severity: critical
spec:
  groups:
  - name: anihpj-hubble-http
    rules:
    - alert: AnihpjHighHTTP500Rate
      expr: |
        rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj",status="500"}[5m])
        /
        rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj"}[5m])
        > 0.05
      for: 5m
      labels:
        severity: critical
        team: anihpj
      annotations:
        summary: "anihpj HTTP 500 error rate > 5%"
        description: "anihpj namespace has {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} HTTP 500 error rate (threshold: 5%)"
        runbook_url: "https://wiki.internal/anihpj-500-runbook"
EOF
kubectl apply -f hubble-alert-rule.yaml

# Fix 2: Verify Prometheus picks up the rule
kubectl get prometheusrule -n monitoring anihpj-hubble-http-alerts

# Fix 3: Check the rule is loaded
curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/rules | jq '.data.groups[] | select(.name=="anihpj-hubble-http")'

# Fix 4: Check alert state
curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/alerts | jq '.data.alerts[] | select(.labels.alertname=="AnihpjHighHTTP500Rate")'
✓

✅ Verify — Alert Fires When HTTP 500 Rate Exceeds 5%

After creating the PrometheusRule CRD with the error ratio expression, Prometheus evaluates it every evaluation interval. When rate(hubble_http_requests_total{status="500"}[5m]) / rate(hubble_http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05 holds for 5 minutes, the alert transitions from PENDING to FIRING. Alertmanager routes the notification based on severity and team labels.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
rate(hubble_http_requests_total{status="500"}[5m]) → non-zero
②
Prometheus rules → no Hubble rules
③
No PrometheusRule CRD for Hubble alerts
④
Create PrometheusRule with error ratio expression
⑤
Alert fires → Alertmanager routes notification

Tenet: Hubble metrics enable precise, application-layer alerting. The key pattern: compare rate(error_metric[5m]) / rate(total_metric[5m]) for error ratios. Use for: 5m to avoid flapping from transient spikes. Hubble metrics labels (status, method, path, namespace, pod) allow targeted alerts — alert on 500s for /api/ paths specifically, or exclude health-check endpoints from alert evaluation.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/rules | jq '.data.groups[].name' | grep -i hubble (empty — no Hubble alerting rules)
$ kubectl get prometheusrule -A No resources found ← No PrometheusRules defined!
$ curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj",status="500"}[5m]) / rate(hubble_http_requests_total{namespace="anihpj"}[5m])' {"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{},"value":[1702,"0.075"]}]}} ← 7.5% — above 5% threshold! But no alert fires.
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get prometheusrule -n monitoring anihpj-hubble-http-alerts NAME AGE anihpj-hubble-http-alerts 2m ✅ Alert rule deployed!
$ curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/rules | jq '.data.groups[] | select(.name=="anihpj-hubble-http") | .rules[].name' "AnihpjHighHTTP500Rate" ✅ Rule loaded in Prometheus
$ curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/alerts | jq '.data.alerts[] | select(.labels.alertname=="AnihpjHighHTTP500Rate") | {state, value}' {state: "firing", value: "0.075"} ✅ Alert FIRING at 7.5%!

Install Cilium from Scratch on EKS with anihpj Deployment

The Problem: You are setting up a new EKS cluster for anihpj. Cilium installation via Helm fails with node initialization errors. Pods stay in Pending state and Cilium agents crash. Your job: install Cilium correctly on EKS, accounting for AWS-specific networking requirements.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# ❌ BUG: Default Helm install fails on EKS
helm repo add cilium https://helm.cilium.io/
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system

# Check Cilium status — agents not ready
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium
# NAME           READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
# cilium-xxxxx   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   5

# Deploy anihpj — pods stuck Pending
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# NAME       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
# web-xxx    0/1     Pending   0      ← Stuck!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. EKS cluster running: kubectl get nodes → 2+ nodes Ready ✅
✓2. Helm installed: helm version → v3.x ✅
✗3. Cilium pods crash: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → CrashLoopBackOff ❌
✗4. anihpj pods Pending: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → Status: Pending — no CNI ❌
✗5. Cilium agent logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium → "Unable to set up ENI mode — AWS API access denied" ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Cilium agent logs for EKS errors: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i error
→ Failed to initialize ENI datapath — Cilium defaults to ENI mode on EKS but the node's IAM role lacks EC2:DescribeNetworkInterfaces permission
2Verify AWS VPC CNI is installed (EKS default): kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node
→ AWS VPC CNI (aws-node) is running — Cilium must either replace it or chain with it
3Check IAM permissions for worker node role: aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name
→ Node role missing AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy — required for ENI/IPAM mode, OR the role exists but lacks EC2:AssignPrivateIpAddresses
4Check Cilium ConfigMap for ENI settings: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep -i eni
→ eni: "true" is set — but EKS with managed node groups requires proper IAM and security group setup
5Root cause identified: Default Helm install uses ENI IPAM mode on EKS without required IAM permissions
→ Cilium auto-detects EKS and enables ENI (Elastic Network Interface) IPAM mode. This requires: 1) IAM role with EC2 permissions on worker nodes, 2) AWS VPC CNI removal or chaining config, and 3) subnet tags for auto-discovery. Missing any of these causes agent crash
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cilium Installed on EKS

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Reinstall Cilium with EKS-specific values
helm uninstall cilium -n kube-system
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set ipam.mode=cluster-pool \
  --set ipam.operator.clusterPoolIPv4PodCIDRList="10.0.0.0/16" \
  --set routingMode=native \
  --set enable-endpoint-routes=true \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=disabled \
  --set nodeinit.enabled=true \
  --set nodeinit.reconfigureKubelet=true

# Fix 2: Wait for Cilium to be ready
cilium status --wait
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium --timeout=300s

# Fix 3: Verify anihpj pods get IPs
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
✓

✅ Verify — Cilium Installed on EKS with anihpj Running

Cilium is installed with ipam.mode=cluster-pool (not ENI mode) and routingMode=native for direct VPC routing. The nodeinit component configures kubelet to use Cilium. All Cilium agents are healthy. anihpj pods transition from Pending to Running with IPs from the cluster-pool CIDR. hubble observe -n anihpj shows FORWARDED flows between web and api pods.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Helm install cilium → agents CrashLoop
②
Logs show ENI/AWS API access denied
③
Check IAM role → missing EC2 permissions
④
Switch ipam.mode to cluster-pool
⑤
Reinstall → agents healthy → anihpj pods Running

Tenet: On EKS, Cilium auto-detects the platform and defaults to ENI IPAM mode (ipam.mode=eni). This requires proper IAM roles, security groups, and subnet tags. For simpler setups, use ipam.mode=cluster-pool with routingMode=native. The nodeinit component is essential — it reconfigures kubelet's CNI config to point to Cilium. Without it, kubelet cannot assign pod IPs.

Debug Cilium Install Failing on AKS Due to Network Plugin Conflict

The Problem: You try to install Cilium on an existing AKS cluster, but Cilium agents fail to start. The Azure CNI is already running and there's a network plugin conflict. Your job: resolve the CNI conflict and install Cilium correctly on AKS.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# ❌ BUG: Installing Cilium on AKS with Azure CNI still active
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system

# Agents crash — network plugin conflict
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium
# NAME           READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
# cilium-xxxxx   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   3

# Azure CNI still running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=azure-cni
# NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
# azure-cni-xxxxx   1/1     Running   0
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. AKS cluster running: kubectl get nodes → 2+ nodes Ready ✅
✓2. Helm v3 available: helm version → OK ✅
✗3. Cilium agents CrashLoop: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → CrashLoopBackOff ❌
✗4. Azure CNI still active: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=azure-cni → Running alongside Cilium ❌
✗5. Cilium logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium → "Cannot start: another CNI plugin detected on node" ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check for Azure CNI DaemonSet: kubectl get ds -n kube-system azure-cni
→ Azure CNI DaemonSet is running — AKS clusters use Azure CNI by default for pod networking
2Check CNI config directory: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ls /etc/cni/net.d/
→ /etc/cni/net.d/ contains 10-azure.conflist — Azure CNI config takes precedence over Cilium's 05-cilium.conflist
3Verify AKS network plugin mode: az aks show -g -n --query networkProfile.networkPlugin
→ networkPlugin: azure — AKS was created with Azure CNI, not 'none' or 'cilium'
4Check if CNI chaining is possible: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep -i chain
→ CNI chaining not configured — Cilium needs to either replace Azure CNI or be configured to chain with it
5Root cause identified: Two CNI plugins (Azure CNI + Cilium) cannot both manage pod networking on the same node
→ Only one CNI plugin can manage pod IP allocation at a time. AKS deploys Azure CNI by default. Cilium detects the existing CNI config and refuses to overwrite it. Solution: either use CNI chaining (Cilium + Azure CNI for IPAM) or recreate the AKS cluster with networkPlugin=none and let Cilium handle everything.
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cilium Installed on AKS

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: For new AKS clusters — create with 'none' CNI
az aks create \
  --resource-group anihpj-rg \
  --name anihpj-aks \
  --network-plugin none \
  --node-count 3

# Fix 2: For existing cluster — use CNI chaining
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set cni.chainingMode=generic-veth \
  --set cni.customConf=true \
  --set ipam.mode=cluster-pool \
  --set ipam.operator.clusterPoolIPv4PodCIDRList="10.0.0.0/16"

# Fix 3: Wait for Cilium and verify
cilium status --wait
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium
✓

✅ Verify — Cilium Running on AKS with CNI Chaining

Cilium is installed with cni.chainingMode=generic-veth, allowing it to coexist with Azure CNI for IPAM while handling policy enforcement and observability. Or, the cluster was recreated with --network-plugin none and Cilium fully manages networking. All Cilium agents are healthy and cilium status shows all components OK.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm install cilium → CrashLoopBackOff
②
Azure CNI DaemonSet still running
③
CNI config conflict in /etc/cni/net.d/
④
Use CNI chaining or recreate with network-plugin=none
⑤
Cilium agents healthy → anihpj deploys

Tenet: AKS has two paths for Cilium: CNI chaining (Cilium sits on top of Azure CNI for policy/observability, Azure CNI handles IPAM) or BYOCNI (Bring Your Own CNI — create cluster with --network-plugin none). CNI chaining is simpler for existing clusters but limits some Cilium features (no KPR, no native routing). BYOCNI gives full Cilium capabilities but requires cluster recreation.

Migrate from Calico to Cilium with Zero Downtime for anihpj

The Problem: Your anihpj production cluster runs Calico as the CNI, but you need to migrate to Cilium without downtime. Simply deleting Calico and installing Cilium causes all pods to lose networking. Your job: perform a zero-downtime CNI migration from Calico to Cilium while anihpj stays online.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Current state: Calico is the CNI
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node
# NAME                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
# calico-node-xxxxx   1/1     Running   0

# anihpj is running on Calico
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: Naive migration = downtime
kubectl delete -f calico.yaml  # Removes Calico — all pods lose networking!
helm install cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system
# Pods are broken during the gap between Calico removal and Cilium readiness
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Calico running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node → All Running ✅
✓2. anihpj deployed on Calico: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide → Running with Calico IPs ✅
✗3. Delete Calico directly: kubectl delete -f calico.yaml → All pods lose IP connectivity immediately! ❌
✗4. New pods fail: After Calico removal, no CNI available — kubelet cannot assign pod IPs ❌
✗5. Existing pods lose networking: Calico's routes and iptables rules are removed, disrupting existing connections ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Understand the migration gap: Between Calico removal and Cilium readiness, there is NO CNI — kubelet cannot create new pods and existing pods lose routes
→ A naive delete-then-install creates a networking outage window — must use Cilium's migration mode
2Check Cilium migration tools: cilium upgrade --from-calico --help
→ Cilium CLI has built-in Calico migration support that imports Calico's IP pools and handles the transition safely
3Verify Calico IP pool configuration: kubectl get ippools.crd.projectcalico.org -o yaml
→ Calico IP pool CIDR must match Cilium's cluster-pool-ipv4-cidr to preserve existing pod IPs
4Check node taint during migration: kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 Taints
→ Nodes should be cordoned one at a time during migration to drain Calico pods and let Cilium take over gracefully
5Root cause identified: Direct Calico deletion creates a CNI vacuum before Cilium is ready
→ CNI migration requires a per-node rollout: cordon node → drain pods → switch CNI config → install Cilium → uncordon. Cilium's cilium-cli automates this with preserve-existing-ips and per-node draining to achieve zero downtime
🔧

🔧 Fix — Zero-Downtime Migration Complete

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix: Zero-downtime migration using Cilium CLI
# Step 1: Deploy Cilium alongside Calico (dual-CNI mode)
cilium install \
  --set ipam.mode=cluster-pool \
  --set ipam.operator.clusterPoolIPv4PodCIDRList="" \
  --set migrate.calico.enabled=true

# Step 2: Cordon and drain each node individually
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do
  kubectl cordon $node
  kubectl drain $node --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
  # CNI switch happens during drain — Cilium takes over
  kubectl uncordon $node
  sleep 30
done

# Step 3: Once all nodes migrated, remove Calico
kubectl delete -f calico.yaml

# Step 4: Verify anihpj never went down
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
✓

✅ Verify — anihpj Running on Cilium with Zero Downtime

The migration is complete. All anihpj pods retained their IPs throughout the migration. kubectl get pods -n anihpj shows pods Running with the same IPs they had under Calico. cilium status shows all agents healthy. Zero request failures during the migration — the per-node cordon-drain-uncordon strategy prevented any outage window.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Calico is current CNI — anihpj running
②
Delete Calico → all pods lose networking
③
Cilium migration mode preserves existing IPs
④
Per-node cordon→drain→switch→uncordon
⑤
All nodes on Cilium → Calico removed → zero downtime

Tenet: The key to zero-downtime CNI migration is per-node draining. You never delete Calico from all nodes at once. Instead: cordon one node, drain its pods (they reschedule on other Calico-managed nodes), switch that node's CNI to Cilium, uncordon. Repeat for each node. Cilium's migrate.calico.enabled flag ensures it configures the same pod CIDR so IPs don't change. Only after ALL nodes are on Cilium do you delete Calico.

$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide NAME READY STATUS IP NODE web-xxx 1/1 Running 192.168.1.5 node-1 web-yyy 1/1 Running 192.168.2.8 node-2 ← Calico assigned IPs
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide NAME READY STATUS IP NODE web-xxx 1/1 Running 192.168.1.5 node-1 web-yyy 1/1 Running 192.168.2.8 node-2 ← Same IPs after migration! ✅
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE cilium-abcde 1/1 Running 0 5m ✅ Cilium now the CNI
$ cilium status /¯¯\ /¯¯\__/¯¯\ Cilium: OK \__/¯¯\__/ Operator: OK /¯¯\__/¯¯\ Hubble: OK \__/¯¯\__/ ClusterMesh: disabled \__/ All 2 nodes healthy — Calico migrated! ✅

Fix CNI Chaining — Cilium + AWS VPC CNI for anihpj

The Problem: On EKS, you install Cilium alongside AWS VPC CNI for CNI chaining (AWS VPC CNI does IPAM, Cilium does policy). But anihpj pods lose network connectivity after Cilium installation. Some pods get IPs from AWS VPC CNI, others from Cilium — causing a split-brain IPAM scenario.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# EKS cluster with AWS VPC CNI running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node
# aws-node-xxxxx   1/1     Running

# Install Cilium for CNI chaining
helm install cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --set cni.chainingMode=aws-cni \
  --set cni.exclusive=false

# ❌ BUG: anihpj pods get split between CNIs
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
# web-xxx   1/1   Running   192.168.1.5   ← VPC CNI IP (OK)
# web-yyy   1/1   Running   10.0.0.23     ← Cilium IP (WRONG!)
# web-zzz   0/1   Pending   <none>         ← No IP assigned
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. AWS VPC CNI running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node → Running ✅
✓2. Cilium installed: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → Running ✅
✗3. Pods get different IP ranges: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide → mixed 192.168.x (VPC) and 10.0.x (Cilium) IPs! ❌
✗4. Some pods Pending: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → Status: Pending — kubelet can't decide which CNI to use ❌
✗5. Cross-pod connectivity broken: Pods with VPC CNI IPs cannot reach pods with Cilium IPs ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check which CNI configs exist on the node: ls /etc/cni/net.d/ on a worker node
→ Both 10-aws.conflist AND 05-cilium.conflist exist — kubelet picks the lowest numbered config, but both compete for IP allocation
2Verify Cilium chaining mode: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep -A3 cni
→ cni.chainingMode is set but cni.customConf might not be true — Cilium overwrites the AWS CNI config instead of chaining after it
3Check AWS VPC CNI ENI limits: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/aws-node | grep ENI
→ AWS VPC CNI may be exhausted on ENI IPs — some pods get Cilium IPs because AWS CNI can't assign more
4Check Cilium IPAM mode: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep ipam
→ ipam.mode=cluster-pool is active — Cilium is independently allocating IPs from its own pool rather than deferring to AWS CNI
5Root cause identified: Improper CNI chaining config causes dual IPAM allocation
→ CNI chaining requires: 1) cni.chainingMode must match the primary CNI (aws-cni), 2) cni.customConf=true so Cilium doesn't overwrite the primary CNI config, 3) ipam.mode must be set to 'eni' or 'cluster-pool' depending on who owns IPAM, and 4) the primary CNI's config must list Cilium as the chained plugin, not the other way around
🔧

🔧 Fix — CNI Chaining Working Correctly

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix: Proper CNI chaining — Cilium sits AFTER AWS VPC CNI
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set cni.chainingMode=aws-cni \
  --set cni.customConf=true \
  --set cni.configMap=cni-configuration \
  --set ipam.mode=eni \
  --set eni.enabled=true \
  --set egressMasqueradeInterfaces=eth0

# Restart Cilium agents
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status ds/cilium -n kube-system

# Delete and recreate anihpj pods to get proper IPs
kubectl delete pods -n anihpj --all
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -n anihpj --all --timeout=120s
✓

✅ Verify — Cilium and AWS VPC CNI Properly Chained

CNI chaining is properly configured. AWS VPC CNI handles IPAM via ENI — all anihpj pods receive VPC-routable IPs (192.168.x). Cilium sits on top for policy enforcement, observability, and eBPF-based routing. All pods are Running with consistent VPC IPs. Cross-pod connectivity and Hubble flows work correctly.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Dual CNI configs compete for IP allocation
②
Pods get mixed IPs from both CNIs
③
Check cni.chainingMode and ipam.mode
④
Set cni.customConf=true, ipam.mode=eni
⑤
Restart agents → all pods get VPC IPs

Tenet: CNI chaining means Cilium delegates IPAM to the primary CNI (AWS VPC CNI or Azure CNI) while handling policy and observability. The critical settings are: cni.chainingMode (identifies the primary CNI), cni.customConf=true (don't overwrite primary CNI config), and ipam.mode (must match the primary CNI's IPAM — 'eni' for AWS, 'cluster-pool' only if Cilium owns IPAM). Without these aligned, both CNIs compete for IP allocation causing split-brain.

$ kubectl exec -n anihpj web-xxx -- ping 10.0.0.23 PING 10.0.0.23: 56 data bytes (no response) ← Cross-CNI connectivity broken!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide NAME READY STATUS IP NODE web-xxx 1/1 Running 192.168.1.5 node-1 web-yyy 1/1 Running 192.168.2.8 node-2 web-zzz 1/1 Running 192.168.3.11 node-1 ← All VPC IPs! ✅
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj web-xxx -- wget -qO- http://192.168.2.8 <html>...nginx...</html> ✅ Cross-pod connectivity restored!

Debug Cilium Connectivity Test Failures in New Cluster

The Problem: You run cilium connectivity test after a fresh Cilium install, but multiple test scenarios fail. The test reports FAIL for pod-to-pod, pod-to-service, and pod-to-world tests. Your job: diagnose why the connectivity test fails and fix the underlying issues.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Fresh Cilium install completed
cilium status --wait

# ❌ BUG: Connectivity test fails
cilium connectivity test
# [=] Test [pod-to-pod] .............................................. ❌
# [=] Test [pod-to-service] ......................................... ❌
# [=] Test [pod-to-world] ........................................... ❌
# [!] 3 of 8 tests failed
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium status OK: cilium status → all components healthy ✅
✓2. Nodes ready: kubectl get nodes → All Ready ✅
✗3. Connectivity test fails: cilium connectivity test → pod-to-pod, pod-to-service, pod-to-world FAIL ❌
✗4. Test pods stuck: kubectl get pods -n cilium-test → some pods Pending/CrashLoopBackOff ❌
✗5. Hubble shows DROPPED: hubble observe --verdict DROPPED → policy denied or no route to host ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check connectivity test namespace: kubectl get pods -n cilium-test
→ Some test pods in Pending/CrashLoopBackOff — indicates CNI or resource issues, not policy
2Check if DNS is working for test pods: kubectl exec -n cilium-test -- nslookup kubernetes.default
→ DNS resolution fails — CoreDNS pods may not be reachable from the test namespace
3Verify pod-to-pod across nodes: kubectl exec -n cilium-test -- ping
→ Ping fails across nodes — VXLAN tunnel, routing, or firewall blocking cross-node pod traffic
4Check kube-proxy or KPR status: cilium config | grep kubeProxyReplacement
→ KPR is disabled but kube-proxy not running — Services have no backend routing
5Root cause identified: Multiple possible causes based on cluster setup
→ Connectivity test failures are rarely a single issue. Common root causes: 1) MTU mismatch (VXLAN/Geneve overhead), 2) kube-proxy not running alongside KPR=disabled, 3) NetworkPolicy denying test traffic, 4) DNS blocked by policy, or 5) firewall rules between nodes blocking VXLAN port 8472/UDP
🔧

🔧 Fix — Connectivity Test Passes

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Check MTU and adjust for tunnel overhead
MTU=$(ip link show eth0 | grep -oP 'mtu \K[0-9]+')
cilium config set mtu $((MTU - 50))  # 50 bytes for VXLAN overhead

# Fix 2: Ensure kube-proxy is running if KPR is disabled
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
# If not running and KPR disabled → install kube-proxy

# Fix 3: Check for default-deny NetworkPolicies blocking test namespace
kubectl get netpol -A
# If a deny-all exists, create an allow rule for cilium-test

# Fix 4: Check firewall between nodes
# Ensure VXLAN port 8472/UDP is open between all nodes
# iptables -I INPUT -p udp --dport 8472 -j ACCEPT

# Fix 5: Re-run connectivity test
cilium connectivity test
✓

✅ Verify — All Connectivity Tests Passing

All 8 connectivity test scenarios pass: pod-to-pod (intra-node), pod-to-pod (inter-node), pod-to-service, pod-to-world, pod-to-host, DNS, client-egress, and network-perf. cilium connectivity test reports 8/8 PASS. Hubble shows FORWARDED flows between all test pods.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cilium connectivity test → FAIL
②
Check test pods → some Pending/CrashLoop
③
Debug specific failures: MTU, DNS, kube-proxy, firewall
④
Apply targeted fixes for each failure
⑤
Re-run → 8/8 PASS

Tenet: The Cilium connectivity test is the single most important diagnostic. It tests the full networking stack: pod-to-pod, Services, DNS, egress, and performance. When it fails, break it down: if pod-to-pod fails → routing/tunnel issue; if pod-to-service fails → kube-proxy/KPR issue; if DNS fails → CoreDNS reachability; if pod-to-world fails → masquerading/egress. Fix one layer at a time.

Upgrade Cilium from v1.15 to v1.16 with anihpj Running

The Problem: You need to upgrade Cilium from v1.15 to v1.16 on a production cluster running anihpj. After the Helm upgrade, Cilium agents fail to start with new errors and anihpj experiences downtime. Your job: perform a safe rolling upgrade preserving anihpj connectivity.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Current: Cilium v1.15 running, anihpj deployed
cilium version
# cilium-cli: v0.16, cilium image: quay.io/cilium/cilium:v1.15.0

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: Direct Helm upgrade breaks agents
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system --version 1.16.0
# Agents enter CrashLoopBackOff — anihpj loses connectivity!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium v1.15 running: cilium version → v1.15.0 ✅
✓2. anihpj deployed and serving: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → 3/3 Running ✅
✗3. Helm upgrade to v1.16: helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.0 → agents CrashLoopBackOff! ❌
✗4. Agent logs show CRD schema mismatch: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium → "Field 'xyz' not recognized in CRD v2alpha1" ❌
✗5. anihpj pods lose connectivity during agent restart: rolling restart doesn't preserve connections if not drained first ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Cilium upgrade guide for v1.16: cilium upgrade --help | grep -A5 1.16
→ Cilium v1.16 requires CRD migration and deprecated field removal — direct Helm upgrade skips CRD updates
2Check current CRD versions: kubectl get crd | grep cilium | awk '{print $1, $3}'
→ CRDs are at v2alpha1 but v1.16 introduces v2 — the new agents can't reconcile old CRD schema
3Review Helm diff before upgrade: helm diff upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system --version 1.16.0
→ Multiple deprecated values flagged: 'enable-endpoint-routes' removed, 'tunnel' changed, 'identityAllocationMode' renamed
4Check if pre-upgrade steps are needed: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-pre-flight -o yaml 2>/dev/null
→ No pre-flight check run — Cilium v1.16 requires pre-flight validation to detect incompatible configs before upgrade
5Root cause identified: Direct Helm upgrade skips CRD migration and config validation
→ Major Cilium version upgrades (v1.15→v1.16) require: 1) CRD upgrade BEFORE agent upgrade, 2) Removal of deprecated Helm values, 3) Pre-flight validation, and 4) Per-node draining to preserve workload connectivity during agent restart. Skipping any step causes agent crashes and downtime
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cilium v1.16 Running

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix: Safe upgrade with pre-flight and per-node draining
# Step 1: Upgrade CRDs first
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cilium/cilium/v1.16.0/install/kubernetes/cilium/crds/crd-clustermesh.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cilium/cilium/v1.16.0/install/kubernetes/cilium/crds/all-crds.yaml

# Step 2: Run pre-flight check
cilium preflight --version 1.16.0

# Step 3: Helm upgrade with updated values
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --version 1.16.0 \
  --set upgradeCompatibility=1.15 \
  --set routingMode=native \
  --set ipam.mode=cluster-pool

# Step 4: Drain nodes one at a time for zero-downtime
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do
  kubectl cordon $node
  kubectl drain $node --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  sleep 30  # Wait for Cilium agent to restart on node
  kubectl uncordon $node
done

# Step 5: Verify
cilium version
cilium status
✓

✅ Verify — anihpj Running on Cilium v1.16 with Zero Downtime

Cilium is upgraded to v1.16.0. All agents are healthy. cilium version confirms v1.16. anihpj pods maintained connectivity throughout the upgrade thanks to per-node draining. kubectl get pods -n anihpj shows all 3 pods Running with the same IPs. Hubble shows continued FORWARDED flows.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cilium version → v1.15
②
Helm upgrade → CrashLoopBackOff
③
CRD schema mismatch + deprecated values
④
CRD upgrade → pre-flight → Helm with updated values
⑤
Per-node drain → v1.16 running → zero downtime

Tenet: Never upgrade Cilium across minor versions without: 1) Upgrading CRDs first (major versions often add/change CRD fields), 2) Running pre-flight (validates config compatibility), 3) Removing deprecated Helm values (check release notes), and 4) Per-node draining (cordon→drain→restart agent→uncordon). This preserves workload connectivity throughout the upgrade.

$ kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i "crd\\|schema\\|field" level=fatal msg="Failed to register CRD" error="field 'endpointRoutes' not found in v2.CiliumEndpoint" level=fatal msg="CRD schema validation failed" subsys=k8s ← CRD mismatch!
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE web-xxx 0/1 Error 0 30s ← Downtime!

Fix Cilium Status Showing Errors After Helm Upgrade

The Problem: After a Helm upgrade, cilium status reports multiple component errors even though pods appear Running. The Operator reports Controller=Degraded, Hubble Relay shows warnings, and some endpoints are in warning state. Your job: diagnose and fix the status errors.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cilium was upgraded via Helm
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system --version 1.16.0

# Deploy anihpj
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: cilium status shows errors
cilium status
# Operator:       Degraded
# Hubble:         Warning
# Controllers:    1/6 failing
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium pods Running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → All Running ✅
✓2. anihpj pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → All Running ✅
✗3. cilium status shows errors: cilium status → Operator: Degraded, Controllers: failing ❌
✗4. Operator logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/cilium-operator → "Failed to reconcile CRD — schema version mismatch" ❌
✗5. Hubble Relay warnings: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/hubble-relay → "TLS certificate expiring in 30 days" ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Operator logs for CRD reconciliation: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/cilium-operator | grep -i error
→ Failed to update CiliumNode CRD: no matches for kind CiliumNode in version cilium.io/v2 — CRD was not upgraded with Helm
2Check Helm CRD management: helm list -n kube-system | grep cilium
→ Helm upgrade used --skip-crds flag or the chart's CRDs were not applied — Cilium Operator can't reconcile old CRD schema
3Verify all CRDs match agent version: kubectl get crd | grep cilium | awk '{print $1, $2}'
→ ciliumnodes.cilium.io shows STORED version as v2alpha1 but agent expects v2 — version mismatch after upgrade
4Check Hubble TLS certificate expiry: kubectl get secret -n kube-system hubble-server-certs -o yaml | grep -A5 cert
→ Hubble Relay TLS certificates are approaching expiry — the status warning is legitimate and requires cert rotation
5Root cause identified: Post-upgrade status errors stem from CRD version mismatch and stale TLS certificates
→ Helm does not automatically upgrade CRDs during chart upgrade (--skip-crds is default). The Operator sees old CRD schema and reports reconciliation errors. Additionally, Hubble Relay's internal TLS certs have a 90-day validity and flag warnings at 30 days. Both issues require explicit CRD upgrade and cert rotation
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cilium Status All OK

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Manually upgrade CRDs to v2
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cilium/cilium/v1.16.0/install/kubernetes/cilium/crds/all-crds.yaml

# Fix 2: Restart Operator to pick up new CRD schema
kubectl rollout restart deploy/cilium-operator -n kube-system
kubectl wait --for=condition=available deploy/cilium-operator -n kube-system --timeout=120s

# Fix 3: Rotate Hubble TLS certificates
kubectl delete secret -n kube-system hubble-server-certs
kubectl delete secret -n kube-system hubble-relay-client-certs
kubectl rollout restart deploy/hubble-relay -n kube-system
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system

# Fix 4: Verify status
cilium status --wait
✓

✅ Verify — All Cilium Components Reporting Healthy

cilium status shows all components OK. Operator reports Controller=OK with no reconciliation errors. Hubble Relay is healthy with renewed TLS certificates. All anihpj endpoints are in ready state. cilium endpoint list shows all pods with valid identities.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cilium status → Operator Degraded
②
Operator logs → CRD version mismatch
③
CRDs at old version, agent expects new
④
Apply new CRDs → restart Operator
⑤
Refresh TLS certs → all status OK

Tenet: After any Cilium upgrade, always check: 1) CRD versions match the agent version (kubectl get crd | grep cilium), 2) Operator reconciliation is successful (no Degraded state), and 3) TLS certificate expiry for Hubble Relay (90-day validity, warning at 30 days). Helm's default --skip-crds means you must apply CRDs manually during major upgrades.

$ kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/cilium-operator | grep -i "crd\|reconcil" level=error msg="Failed to reconcile CiliumNode" error="no matches for kind CiliumNode in version cilium.io/v2alpha1" subsys=controller level=error msg="CRD schema version mismatch" expected=v2 current=v2alpha1
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix

Configure Cilium with External etcd for anihpj Production

The Problem: For production high availability, you configure Cilium to use an external etcd cluster instead of Kubernetes CRDs. After switching, Cilium agents fail to start — they cannot connect to the external etcd. Your job: debug the etcd connection and fix the configuration.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# External etcd cluster: etcd.anihpj.internal:2379
# Configure Cilium to use external etcd
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --set etcd.enabled=true \
  --set etcd.ssl=true \
  --set etcd.endpoints[0]=https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379

# ❌ BUG: Cilium agents can't connect to etcd
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium
# cilium-xxxxx   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   3

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
# web-xxx   0/1     Pending   ← No CNI available
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. External etcd cluster running: curl -k https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379/version → JSON response ✅
✓2. Helm upgrade applied: helm list -n kube-system | grep cilium → deployed ✅
✗3. Cilium agents CrashLoop: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → CrashLoopBackOff ❌
✗4. Agent logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium → "Failed to connect to etcd: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" ❌
✗5. anihpj pods Pending: No CNI — kubelet cannot assign pod IPs ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Cilium agent etcd connection: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i etcd
→ x509: certificate signed by unknown authority — the etcd server's TLS certificate is not trusted by Cilium agents
2Verify etcd TLS certificates are in Kubernetes secrets: kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-etcd-secrets -o yaml | grep -c data
→ Secret cilium-etcd-secrets does not exist — the external etcd CA cert, client cert, and client key were never provided to Cilium
3Check Helm values for etcd TLS config: helm get values cilium -n kube-system | grep -A10 etcd
→ etcd.ssl=true is set but etcd.ssl.caCert, etcd.ssl.clientCert, and etcd.ssl.clientKey values are empty — TLS is enabled but certificates are missing
4Test etcd connectivity manually from a node: curl --cacert /etc/etcd/ca.crt --cert /etc/etcd/client.crt --key /etc/etcd/client.key https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379/version
→ Manual connection works with proper certs — confirms the issue is missing certs in Cilium's config, not etcd itself
5Root cause identified: TLS is enabled but no certificates provided to Cilium for external etcd
→ When etcd.ssl=true is set, Cilium requires: 1) CA certificate (to verify the etcd server), 2) Client certificate (for mutual TLS), and 3) Client key. These must be provided via Kubernetes TLS secrets and referenced in Helm values (etcd.ssl.caCert, etcd.ssl.clientCert, etcd.ssl.clientKey) or stored in a pre-existing secret named cilium-etcd-secrets
🔧

🔧 Fix — External etcd Connected

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Create Kubernetes TLS secret from etcd certs
kubectl create secret generic cilium-etcd-secrets \
  -n kube-system \
  --from-file=etcd-ca.crt=/etc/etcd/ca.crt \
  --from-file=etcd-client.crt=/etc/etcd/client.crt \
  --from-file=etcd-client.key=/etc/etcd/client.key

# Fix 2: Reconfigure Cilium with etcd certs
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set etcd.ssl=true \
  --set etcd.endpoints[0]=https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379 \
  --set etcd.ssl.caCert=/etc/cilium/etcd-ca.crt \
  --set etcd.ssl.clientCert=/etc/cilium/etcd-client.crt \
  --set etcd.ssl.clientKey=/etc/cilium/etcd-client.key

# Fix 3: Restart Cilium agents
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
cilium status --wait
✓

✅ Verify — Cilium Connected to External etcd

Cilium agents connect to the external etcd cluster via mutual TLS. cilium status shows KVStore: OK with the etcd endpoint. Identities and state are stored in the external etcd. anihpj pods are Running with IPs. etcdctl --endpoints=https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379 get --prefix cilium/ shows Cilium state stored in etcd.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Helm set etcd.enabled=true, etcd.ssl=true
②
Agents CrashLoop → x509: unknown authority
③
No cilium-etcd-secrets → certs not provided
④
Create TLS secret + Helm values for certs
⑤
Restart agents → KVStore OK → anihpj Running

Tenet: External etcd requires three certificates for mutual TLS: CA cert (to verify the etcd server), client cert (to authenticate Cilium to etcd), and client key. These must be loaded from a Kubernetes secret. The Helm values etcd.ssl.caCert, etcd.ssl.clientCert, and etcd.ssl.clientKey specify the file paths inside the Cilium agent container. Without all three, the agent cannot establish a trusted TLS connection and crashes.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i etcd level=fatal msg="Failed to connect to etcd" error="x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" endpoint=https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379 level=fatal msg="Unable to initialize KVStore" subsys=kvstore
$ kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-etcd-secrets Error from server (NotFound): secrets "cilium-etcd-secrets" not found ← No TLS certs!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cilium status | grep -i kvstore KVStore: Ok etcd: 1/1 connected, has-quorum, https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379 (v3.5.0) ✅
$ etcdctl --endpoints=https://etcd.anihpj.internal:2379 get --prefix cilium/state/identities/v1/ --keys-only | head -5 cilium/state/identities/v1/id/1 cilium/state/identities/v1/id/128 cilium/state/identities/v1/id/256 ✅ Cilium state in etcd!
🧹

Debug CiliumEndpointSlice Migration Issues

The Problem: You enable CiliumEndpointSlice (CES) for better scalability, but after enabling, some anihpj endpoints are missing from cilium endpoint list. Hubble doesn't show flows for certain pods. Your job: debug the CES migration and fix endpoint visibility.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Enable CiliumEndpointSlice for scalability
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set bpf.masquerade=true \
  --set endpointSlice.enabled=true

# Deploy anihpj with many pods
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=5
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=5

# ❌ BUG: Some endpoints missing
cilium endpoint list
# Shows only 6 endpoints — but 10 pods exist!
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# 10 pods Running
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium agents Running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → All Running ✅
✓2. CES enabled: kubectl get ciliumendpointslice -A → CES objects exist ✅
✗3. Endpoint count mismatch: cilium endpoint list | wc -l → 6 endpoints for 10 pods! ❌
✗4. Some pods not in CEP: kubectl get cep -n anihpj → only 6 CiliumEndpoints, 4 pods have no CEP ❌
✗5. Hubble missing flows: hubble observe -n anihpj → flows only for 6 pods — 4 are invisible! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check CiliumEndpointSlice objects: kubectl get ces -A
→ CES objects exist but some have fewer endpoints than expected — the migration from per-endpoint CEP to CES may have missed pods created during the transition
2Compare CEP count vs pod count: echo "Pods: $(kubectl get pods -n anihpj --no-headers | wc -l)" && echo "CEPs: $(kubectl get cep -n anihpj --no-headers | wc -l)"
→ Pod count (10) vs CEP count (6) — 4 pods are running without a CiliumEndpoint, meaning no identity or policy applies to them
3Check agent logs for CES sync errors: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i "endpointslice\|ces"
→ CES sync delay: agent's local cache still uses CEP model, CES update from API server is lagging, causing stale endpoint state
4Verify CES identity mapping: kubectl get ces -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 identities
→ CES shows 6 identities but no identity mapping for the 4 missing pods — identity allocation failed during CES transition
5Root cause identified: CES migration leaves endpoints in limbo during the CEP-to-CES transition
→ When CES is enabled on a running cluster, existing CEPs are gradually migrated to CES. During the transition window, new pods may not get registered in either CEP or CES — the agent's endpoint management switches models mid-flight. Restarting Cilium agents forces a clean reconciliation of all endpoints into CES
🔧

🔧 Fix — All Endpoints Visible in CES

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Force Cilium agent restart to reconcile all endpoints into CES
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status ds/cilium -n kube-system --timeout=300s

# Fix 2: Delete stale CEPs to force CES recreation
kubectl delete cep -n anihpj --all

# Fix 3: Verify all pods have CES entries
kubectl get ces -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -c "name:"
# Should match pod count

# Fix 4: Verify endpoints visible
cilium endpoint list
# Should show all 10 endpoints
✓

✅ Verify — All 10 anihpj Pods Have Endpoints in CES

After restarting Cilium agents, all 10 anihpj pods are registered in CiliumEndpointSlice. cilium endpoint list shows all 10 endpoints with valid identities. kubectl get ces -n anihpj shows endpoints grouped by identity. Hubble observes flows for all pods. The CES migration is complete with no missing endpoints.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
10 pods Running → only 6 endpoints
②
Some pods have no CEP → no identity
③
CES sync lag during migration transition
④
Restart agents → force full reconciliation
⑤
All 10 endpoints visible → Hubble sees all

Tenet: CiliumEndpointSlice (CES) groups endpoints by security identity instead of creating one CEP per pod. This dramatically reduces Kubernetes API load at scale (one CES per identity vs one CEP per pod). During CES migration, always restart Cilium agents after enabling to force a clean endpoint reconciliation. Stale CEPs can be safely deleted — the agent will recreate them as CES entries.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj --no-headers | wc -l 10 ← 10 pods running
$ kubectl get cep -n anihpj --no-headers | wc -l 6 ← Only 6 have CiliumEndpoints!
$ cilium endpoint list ENDPOINT POLICY (ingress) POLICY (egress) IDENTITY IPV4 STATUS 1234 Enabled Enabled 128 10.0.1.10 ready 1235 Enabled Enabled 128 10.0.1.11 ready (only 6 of 10 endpoints shown)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cilium endpoint list ENDPOINT POLICY (ingress) POLICY (egress) IDENTITY IPV4 STATUS 1234-1243 10 endpoints shown — all ready ✅ All 10 visible!
$ kubectl get ces -n anihpj NAME AGE anihpj-web 2m anihpj-api 2m ✅ Endpoints grouped by identity in CES
