Fix System Requirements Check Failing — Kernel Too Old for BBR

The Problem: You attempt to enable BBR congestion control and Bandwidth Manager for anihpj, but Cilium agents fail with kernel compatibility errors. The nodes run Ubuntu 20.04 with kernel 5.4 — too old for BBR. Your job: verify system requirements and fix the configuration to work with the available kernel.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Try to enable Bandwidth Manager with BBR
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set bandwidthManager.enabled=true \
  --set bandwidthManager.bbr=true

# ❌ BUG: Agents crash — kernel too old
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium
# cilium-xxxxx   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   5

kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i bbr
# "BBR requires kernel 5.18+ — current kernel: 5.4.0"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium installed: cilium version → OK ✅
✓2. Nodes available: kubectl get nodes → 3 Ready ✅
✗3. Agents CrashLoop: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → CrashLoopBackOff after enabling BBR ❌
✗4. Kernel version check: uname -r on node → 5.4.0 — too old for BBR (needs 5.18+) ❌
✗5. Bandwidth Manager also fails: requires BPF Host Routing which needs kernel 5.10+ with specific config ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check kernel version on all nodes: kubectl get nodes -o wide && kubectl debug node/ --image=busybox -- uname -r
→ All nodes running kernel 5.4.0 — Cilium BBR requires 5.18+, Bandwidth Manager requires 5.10+ with BTF and BPF Host Routing
2Check kernel features available: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium kernel-check
→ Missing: CONFIG_TCP_CONG_BBR not compiled, BTF not available, BPF Host Routing unsupported — multiple kernel config requirements not met
3Verify Cilium minimum requirements: cilium status | grep -i kernel
→ Cilium itself supports kernel 5.4 but specific features (BBR, BW Mgr, KPR strict) have higher requirements
4Check if BTF is available: ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux 2>/dev/null
→ BTF missing — kernel was not compiled with CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF=y, which is required for CO-RE and many BPF features
5Root cause identified: Feature-specific kernel requirements not met — kernel 5.4 is too old for BBR and Bandwidth Manager
→ Cilium features have tiered kernel requirements: Basic CNI works on 5.4+, KPR needs 5.10+, Bandwidth Manager needs 5.10+ with BTF and BPF Host Routing, BBR needs 5.18+. The kernel check command (cilium kernel-check) validates each node's kernel config against the enabled features
🔧

🔧 Fix — BBR Disabled Gracefully

BASH — apply the fix 
# Fix 1: Disable BBR — fall back to EDT (Earliest Departure Time)
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set bandwidthManager.enabled=true \
  --set bandwidthManager.bbr=false

# Fix 2: Verify Bandwidth Manager works without BBR (if kernel >= 5.10)
# If kernel is 5.4, disable Bandwidth Manager entirely:
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set bandwidthManager.enabled=false

# Fix 3 (long term): Upgrade kernel to 5.18+ for full BBR support
# Ubuntu 22.04+ or kernel 5.18+ via HWE
apt-get install linux-generic-hwe-22.04

# Fix 4: Run kernel check after changes
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium kernel-check
✓

✅ Verify — Cilium Running with Kernel-Compatible Features

Cilium agents are healthy with feature set matching the available kernel. cilium kernel-check shows which features are compatible. Bandwidth Manager uses EDT (Earliest Departure Time) instead of BBR — still functional for bandwidth limiting. If kernel is 5.4, Bandwidth Manager is disabled and Cilium runs in basic CNI mode. All anihpj pods are Running.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Enable BBR → agents CrashLoopBackOff
②
Check kernel: 5.4 → BBR needs 5.18+
③
cilium kernel-check → missing BTF + BBR
④
Disable BBR → use EDT or disable BW Mgr
⑤
Agents healthy → anihpj Running

Tenet: Always run cilium kernel-check before enabling advanced features. Cilium's tiered requirements: 5.4+ for basic CNI, 5.10+ with BTF for KPR/BW Manager/eBPF Host Routing, 5.18+ for BBR. When kernel is too old, gracefully degrade feature set rather than forcing agent crashes. Use EDT (Earliest Departure Time) as BBR alternative — it provides fair queueing without kernel 5.18+.

🧪 SCENARIO S75 — Category 6: Cluster Mesh

Set Up Cluster Mesh Between anihpj-us and anihpj-eu

The Problem: You need to connect two anihpj clusters (us-east and eu-west) via Cilium Cluster Mesh. After running cilium clustermesh connect, the clusters fail to establish a connection. Hubble shows no cross-cluster flows. Your job: set up Cluster Mesh correctly and verify cross-cluster service discovery.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cluster 1: anihpj-us (context: us-east)
kubectl config use-context us-east
cilium install --cluster-name anihpj-us --cluster-id 1

# Cluster 2: anihpj-eu (context: eu-west)
kubectl config use-context eu-west
cilium install --cluster-name anihpj-eu --cluster-id 2

# Deploy anihpj in both clusters
for ctx in us-east eu-west; do
  kubectl config use-context $ctx
  kubectl create namespace anihpj
  kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
  kubectl expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80 --name=web-service
done

# ❌ BUG: Cluster Mesh connection fails
cilium clustermesh connect --context us-east --destination-context eu-west
# Error: Unable to establish connection — TLS handshake failed
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Both clusters running Cilium: cilium status → OK on both clusters ✅
✓2. Unique cluster names/IDs: cilium config | grep cluster → cluster-id=1 (us), cluster-id=2 (eu) ✅
✗3. Cluster Mesh connect fails: cilium clustermesh connect → TLS handshake failed — connection refused ❌
✗4. Cross-cluster pod ping: kubectl exec -n anihpj web-us-xxx -- ping web-eu-service.anihpj.svc → unknown host ❌
✗5. Hubble shows no cross-cluster flows: hubble observe --cluster anihpj-eu → no flows from remote cluster ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Cluster Mesh status: cilium clustermesh status --context us-east
→ Cluster Mesh: disconnected — clusters cannot see each other; the clustermesh-apiserver service may not be accessible between clusters
2Verify clustermesh-apiserver is running: kubectl get svc -n kube-system clustermesh-apiserver
→ Service exists as ClusterIP only — remote clusters cannot reach it; needs to be exposed via LoadBalancer or NodePort for cross-cluster access
3Check TLS certificates for cross-cluster auth: kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-ca -o yaml | grep -c cert
→ Each cluster has its own CA — but the clusters don't trust each other's CA certificates; mutual TLS requires shared CA or cross-signed certificates
4Verify network connectivity between clusters: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- curl -k https://:2379/version
→ Connection timeout — firewall or network policy is blocking inter-cluster traffic on the etcd port (2379)
5Root cause identified: Cluster Mesh requires exposed apiserver, shared CA trust, and open network paths between clusters
→ Three requirements for Cluster Mesh: 1) clustermesh-apiserver must be accessible from the remote cluster (LoadBalancer/NodePort, not just ClusterIP), 2) Both clusters must share the same CA certificate for mutual TLS authentication, and 3) Network connectivity must exist between cluster nodes (firewall rules allowing ports 2379 and 4240)
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cross-Cluster Service Discovery

BASH — cross-cluster service discovery 
# Fix 1: Export CA from us-east and import into eu-west
kubectl config use-context us-east
kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-ca -o yaml > us-ca.yaml
# Edit: change namespace to kube-system, rename to cilium-ca
kubectl config use-context eu-west
kubectl apply -f us-ca.yaml

# Fix 2: Expose clustermesh-apiserver via LoadBalancer
kubectl patch svc -n kube-system clustermesh-apiserver \
  -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
# Do this on BOTH clusters

# Fix 3: Connect Cluster Mesh with shared CA
cilium clustermesh connect \
  --context us-east \
  --destination-context eu-west

# Fix 4: Verify connection
cilium clustermesh status --context us-east
✓

✅ Verify — Cluster Mesh Connected Between anihpj-us and anihpj-eu

Cluster Mesh is established. cilium clustermesh status shows connected with both clusters listed. kubectl exec -n anihpj web-us-xxx -- curl web-service.anihpj.svc resolves to the global service across both clusters. Hubble shows cross-cluster flows with remote cluster labels. anihpj services are discoverable from either cluster.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cilium clustermesh connect → TLS handshake failed
②
clustermesh-apiserver is ClusterIP only
③
Different CAs per cluster → no mutual TLS trust
④
Share CA → expose LoadBalancer → connect
⑤
Cross-cluster service resolution works

Tenet: Cluster Mesh requires three prerequisites: 1) Shared CA certificate — both clusters must trust the same CA for mutual TLS between clustermesh-apiservers, 2) Exposed apiserver — clustermesh-apiserver must be reachable from the remote cluster (LoadBalancer, NodePort, or routable IP), and 3) Network path — firewalls must allow etcd (2379) and health-check (4240) ports between clusters. Without any one of these, the mesh cannot form.

S76
🧪 SCENARIO S76 — Category 6: Cluster Mesh

Debug Cluster Mesh Not Connecting — TLS Certificate Mismatch

The Problem: You established Cluster Mesh but periodically the connection drops. Cilium agents log TLS errors. The mesh works initially but breaks after certificate rotation. Your job: diagnose the TLS certificate mismatch and fix the Cluster Mesh authentication.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cluster Mesh was working, now disconnected
cilium clustermesh status --context us-east
# anihpj-us: OK, anihpj-eu: TLS_ERROR

# Deploy anihpj for testing
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2

# ❌ BUG: Cross-cluster connections failing with TLS errors
kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i tls
# "x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Both clusters have Cilium running: cilium status → OK ✅
✓2. Cluster Mesh was previously working: cilium clustermesh status → previously connected ✅
✗3. Mesh now shows TLS error: cilium clustermesh status → anihpj-eu: TLS_ERROR — certificate validation failed ❌
✗4. Agent logs show expiry: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep x509 → certificate has expired ❌
✗5. Cross-cluster services unreachable: kubectl exec -n anihpj web-us-xxx -- curl web-service.anihpj.svc.global → connection refused ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Cilium CA certificate expiry: kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-ca -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates
→ CA certificate expired 2 days ago — Cilium's internal CA has a default 1-year validity; after expiry, all TLS connections between clusters fail
2Check clustermesh-apiserver certificate: kubectl get secret -n kube-system clustermesh-apiserver-server-cert -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates
→ Server certificate also expired — tied to the same CA; cert-manager or manual rotation is needed
3Verify both clusters use the same CA: diff <(kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-ca -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' --context us-east) <(kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-ca -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' --context eu-west)
→ CA certificates differ — one cluster rotated its CA but the other still has the old CA; the clusters no longer trust each other
4Check if cert-manager is managing Cilium certs: kubectl get certificate -n kube-system | grep cilium
→ No Certificate resources — Cilium's built-in CA auto-generates certs but does NOT auto-renew them; manual rotation or cert-manager integration is required for production
5Root cause identified: Cilium internal CA certificates expire after 1 year with no auto-renewal
→ Cilium generates a self-signed CA during installation. All Cluster Mesh TLS certs (clustermesh-apiserver, remote, admin) are signed by this CA with a 1-year validity. When the CA or any certificate expires, all cross-cluster TLS connections fail. Production clusters need either cert-manager integration or manual certificate rotation before expiry
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cluster Mesh Reconnected

BASH — cluster mesh reconnected 
# Fix 1: Rotate CA on both clusters with matching cert
# Generate new CA (do once, share between clusters)
openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -nodes \
  -out ca.crt -keyout ca.key \
  -subj "/CN=cilium-ca"

# Update CA secret on BOTH clusters
for ctx in us-east eu-west; do
  kubectl --context $ctx delete secret -n kube-system cilium-ca
  kubectl --context $ctx create secret generic cilium-ca \
    -n kube-system --from-file=ca.crt --from-file=ca.key
done

# Fix 2: Restart Cilium components to pick up new CA
for ctx in us-east eu-west; do
  kubectl --context $ctx rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
  kubectl --context $ctx rollout restart deploy/clustermesh-apiserver -n kube-system
done

# Fix 3: Re-establish Cluster Mesh
cilium clustermesh connect --context us-east --destination-context eu-west
✓

✅ Verify — TLS Certificates Rotated and Mesh Restored

Both clusters now trust the renewed CA certificate (valid for 10 years). cilium clustermesh status shows both clusters connected with OK status. Cross-cluster service resolution works. Agent logs show successful TLS handshakes. The shared CA ensures both clusters trust each other for mutual TLS.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Mesh was working → now TLS_ERROR
②
Check CA cert → expired 2 days ago
③
Cilium CA has 1-year validity, no auto-renew
④
Generate new shared CA → update both clusters
⑤
Restart agents → Mesh reconnects

Tenet: Cilium's internal CA auto-generates during install but never auto-renews. The CA and all derived certificates (clustermesh-apiserver, remote, admin) share a 1-year lifespan. For production: either integrate cert-manager to auto-renew, or set up monitoring to alert 30 days before expiry. When rotating, always share the SAME CA between both clusters — different CAs break mutual TLS trust.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ cilium clustermesh status --context us-east Cluster Mesh: connected (1/2) anihpj-us (cluster-id: 1): OK anihpj-eu (cluster-id: 2): TLS_ERROR — x509: certificate has expired ❌
$ kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-ca -o jsonpath="{.data.ca\.crt}" | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates notBefore=Jun 3 2025 12:00:00 GMT notAfter=Jun 3 2026 12:00:00 GMT ← Expired 2 days ago!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get secret -n kube-system cilium-ca -o jsonpath="{.data.ca\.crt}" | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates notBefore=Jun 3 2026 12:00:00 GMT notAfter=Jun 3 2036 12:00:00 GMT ✅ 10-year validity!
$ cilium clustermesh status --context us-east Cluster Mesh: connected (2/2) anihpj-us (cluster-id: 1): OK anihpj-eu (cluster-id: 2): OK ✅ TLS restored!

Fix Global Service Not Resolving Across Clusters

The Problem: Cluster Mesh is connected, but anihpj services are not discoverable across clusters. web-service.anihpj.svc.global returns NXDOMAIN. Pods in us-east cannot reach services in eu-west. Your job: enable global service discovery and fix cross-cluster DNS resolution.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cluster Mesh connected, but global services failing
cilium clustermesh status --context us-east
# Both clusters: OK

# Deploy anihpj in both clusters
kubectl --context us-east create namespace anihpj
kubectl --context us-east create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl --context us-east expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80 --name=web-service

kubectl --context eu-west create namespace anihpj
kubectl --context eu-west create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl --context eu-west expose deployment web -n anihpj --port=80 --name=web-service

# ❌ BUG: Global service not resolving
kubectl --context us-east exec -n anihpj web-xxx -- nslookup web-service.anihpj.svc.global
# server can't find web-service.anihpj.svc.global: NXDOMAIN
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cluster Mesh connected: cilium clustermesh status → both clusters OK ✅
✓2. Local services resolve: nslookup web-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → resolves locally ✅
✗3. Global service NXDOMAIN: nslookup web-service.anihpj.svc.global → NXDOMAIN — no global record ❌
✗4. Cross-cluster curl fails: curl web-service.anihpj.svc.global → Could not resolve host ❌
✗5. No global services listed: cilium service list | grep global → empty ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if the service is annotated as global: kubectl get svc -n anihpj web-service -o yaml | grep -i global
→ No global annotation — services are local by default; must add io.cilium/global-service: "true" annotation to expose across clusters
2Verify service is annotated on BOTH clusters: for ctx in us-east eu-west; do kubectl --context $ctx get svc -n anihpj web-service -o yaml | grep io.cilium/global-service; done
→ Neither cluster has the annotation — both need io.cilium/global-service: "true" for cross-cluster discovery
3Check Cilium global service list: cilium service list | grep -A5 global
→ No global services registered — the annotation triggers Cilium to register the service in the global service registry shared via Cluster Mesh
4Verify shared service identity across clusters: kubectl --context us-east get cep -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 identity && kubectl --context eu-west get cep -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 identity
→ Pods in different clusters have different identity IDs — global services use identity-based backend selection; identities must be consistent
5Root cause identified: Services are not annotated as global — Cluster Mesh does not auto-export services
→ Cluster Mesh connects clusters but does NOT automatically make services global. Each Service must be explicitly annotated with io.cilium/global-service: "true" on ALL clusters that should share it. Without this annotation, services remain local to their cluster and .svc.global DNS resolution fails with NXDOMAIN
🔧

🔧 Fix — Global Service Resolution

BASH — global service resolution 
# Fix 1: Annotate services as global on BOTH clusters
for ctx in us-east eu-west; do
  kubectl --context $ctx annotate svc -n anihpj web-service \
    io.cilium/global-service=true \
    io.cilium/shared-service=true --overwrite
done

# Fix 2: Verify global service appears
sleep 10  # Wait for Cluster Mesh to sync
cilium service list | grep global

# Fix 3: Test cross-cluster resolution
kubectl --context us-east exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- nslookup web-service.anihpj.svc.global

# Fix 4: Test cross-cluster connectivity
kubectl --context us-east exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s http://web-service.anihpj.svc.global
✓

✅ Verify — Cross-Cluster Service Discovery Working

web-service.anihpj.svc.global resolves to backend pods in both clusters. cilium service list shows the service as GLOBAL with backends from us-east AND eu-west. Requests are load-balanced across all backend pods regardless of which cluster they reside in.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Cluster Mesh connected but .svc.global NXDOMAIN
②
Check annotation → no io.cilium/global-service
③
Services are local by default
④
Annotate both clusters → service registered as global
⑤
.svc.global resolves → cross-cluster LB works

Tenet: Cluster Mesh provides the infrastructure for cross-cluster connectivity, but global services are opt-in. Each Service needs io.cilium/global-service: "true" annotation on ALL participating clusters. Use io.cilium/shared-service: "true" for services that exist in multiple clusters (shared identity). DNS resolution via .svc.global suffix is handled by Cilium's internal DNS proxy, not CoreDNS.

Debug Cross-Cluster Pod-to-Pod Connectivity Failure

The Problem: Cluster Mesh is connected, but pods in us-east cannot ping pods in eu-west directly. Global services work, but direct pod-to-pod IP communication across clusters fails. Your job: debug why cross-cluster pod IP routing is broken.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cluster Mesh connected, global services work
cilium clustermesh status
# Both clusters: OK

# Deploy pods in both clusters
kubectl --context us-east create namespace anihpj
kubectl --context us-east run debug-us -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl --context eu-west create namespace anihpj
kubectl --context eu-west run debug-eu -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine

# Get pod IPs
US_IP=$(kubectl --context us-east get pod debug-us -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
EU_IP=$(kubectl --context eu-west get pod debug-eu -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')

kubectl --context us-east exec -n anihpj debug-us -- ping -c3 $EU_IP
# 100% packet loss — no route to host
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cluster Mesh connected: cilium clustermesh status → both OK ✅
✓2. Local pod-to-pod works: ping → success within same cluster ✅
✗3. Cross-cluster pod ping fails: ping → 100% packet loss, no route to host ❌
✗4. No cross-cluster routes: ip route | grep → no route to remote pod CIDR ❌
✗5. Hubble shows DROPPED: hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/debug-us --to-ip $EU_IP → DROPPED — no tunnel to remote cluster ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if tunnel is established between clusters: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium bpf tunnel list | grep
→ No tunnel entries for remote cluster — Cilium uses VXLAN or Geneve tunnels between clusters; if the tunnel mesh is not established, pod IPs are not routable
2Verify pod CIDR routing between clusters: ip route show | grep
→ No route to remote pod CIDR — Cilium should install routes to remote cluster pod CIDRs via the tunnel interface
3Check CiliumNode resources for remote cluster: kubectl get ciliumnode -l io.cilium/cluster=
→ No CiliumNode resources from remote cluster — Cluster Mesh syncs CiliumNode CRDs between clusters; if they're missing, the local cluster doesn't know about remote node IPs and pod CIDRs
4Verify etcd or CRD sync is working: etcdctl get --prefix cilium/state/nodes/v2/
→ Remote cluster node entries not synced — the Cluster Mesh etcd sync may be incomplete or failing due to network issues
5Root cause identified: Cross-cluster pod IP routing requires tunnel mesh and route propagation via Cluster Mesh etcd
→ Direct pod-to-pod communication across clusters requires: 1) Tunnel mesh between all nodes in both clusters (VXLAN/Geneve), 2) Route propagation via shared etcd (each cluster publishes its pod CIDRs), and 3) No firewall blocking the tunnel port (8472/UDP for VXLAN) between cluster nodes. If any of these is missing, cross-cluster pod IPs are unreachable
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cross-Cluster Pod Connectivity

BASH — cross-cluster pod connectivity 
# Fix 1: Verify and fix tunnel mesh configuration
cilium config set tunnel=vxlan
cilium config set tunnel-port=8472

# Fix 2: Ensure firewall allows VXLAN between clusters
# AWS: Update security groups to allow UDP 8472 between cluster nodes
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-xxx --protocol udp --port 8472 \
  --source-group sg-yyy

# Fix 3: Force Cluster Mesh re-sync
kubectl --context us-east delete pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium
kubectl --context eu-west delete pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium
# Wait for agents to restart and re-establish tunnels

# Fix 4: Verify routes appear
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ip route | grep
✓

✅ Verify — Direct Pod-to-Pod Routing Across Clusters

Pods in us-east can now ping pods in eu-west by IP. ip route shows routes to remote cluster pod CIDRs via the Cilium tunnel interface. cilium bpf tunnel list shows tunnel endpoints for all remote cluster nodes. Hubble shows FORWARDED flows for cross-cluster pod-to-pod traffic.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Direct pod IP ping across clusters fails
②
Check routes → no route to remote CIDR
③
Tunnel mesh not established between clusters
④
Open firewall UDP 8472 + restart agents
⑤
Routes appear → cross-cluster ping works

Tenet: Cross-cluster pod-to-pod routing relies on tunnel mesh between ALL nodes across clusters. Cilium uses the same VXLAN/Geneve tunnel it uses within a cluster, extended across Cluster Mesh. The tunnel port (8472/UDP) must be open between all nodes in both clusters. Routes to remote pod CIDRs are propagated via the Cluster Mesh etcd and installed by each Cilium agent. Without route propagation, even if tunnels exist, traffic won't be forwarded.

The Problem: You need to restrict cross-cluster traffic — anihpj-us pods should only access anihpj-eu API, not the database. But CiliumNetworkPolicy doesn't apply across clusters. Your job: create cross-cluster network policies for anihpj traffic.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cluster Mesh connected, anihpj global services work
# Deploy anihpj in both clusters

# ❌ BUG: CNP applied to us-east doesn't restrict eu-west traffic
kubectl --context us-east apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:

  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels: {tier: api}
EOF
# Policy only applies to local cluster — eu-west pods can still access us-east db!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cluster Mesh connected: cilium clustermesh status → OK ✅
✓2. CNP applied locally: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj restrict-db → deployed ✅
✗3. Verify policy blocks local: local non-api pod blocked from db ✅ — but remote cluster non-api pod reaches db! ❌
✗4. Check remote pod access: kubectl --context eu-west exec deploy/web -- curl db-service.anihpj.svc.global:5432 → CONNECTED — policy not enforced across clusters! ❌
✗5. Policy only in local cluster: cilium policy get → restrict-db applies locally but not to remote cluster traffic ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if CCNP (cluster-wide) was used instead of CNP: kubectl get ccnp restrict-db
→ No CCNP exists — CNP is namespace-scoped and local to one cluster; cross-cluster policies require CCNP (CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy) which applies across all clusters in the mesh
2Verify the CNP is only in one cluster: for ctx in us-east eu-west; do kubectl --context $ctx get cnp -n anihpj restrict-db 2>/dev/null; done
→ CNP exists only in us-east — policies are NOT automatically synced across Cluster Mesh; each cluster manages its own policies
3Check if identity-based policy works across clusters: cilium identity list | grep anihpj
→ Identities are local per cluster — us-east identity 128 for 'tier=db' is different from eu-west identity 256 for 'tier=db'. Cross-cluster identity mapping is needed
4Create CCNP for cross-cluster enforcement: kubectl apply -f ccnp-cross-cluster.yaml
→ CCNP with cluster scope applies to all clusters — but it must be created on EACH cluster where enforcement is desired, or the policy must use global identity references
5Root cause identified: CNP is namespace and cluster scoped — cross-cluster policy requires CCNP on all clusters
→ CiliumNetworkPolicy (CNP) is namespaced and applies only to the local cluster. For cross-cluster policy enforcement, you need: 1) CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (CCNP) on all clusters, 2) Consistent labels across clusters (same labels = same identity via Cluster Mesh), and 3) The policy must reference identities, not endpoints, for cross-cluster matching
🔧

🔧 Fix — Cross-Cluster Policy Enforcement

BASH — cross-cluster policy enforcement 
# Fix: Create CCNP on BOTH clusters for cross-cluster enforcement
cat > ccnp-cross-cluster.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-db-cross-cluster
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
      tier: db
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
        tier: api
    - matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
        tier: web
EOF

for ctx in us-east eu-west; do
  kubectl --context $ctx apply -f ccnp-cross-cluster.yaml
done

# Verify policy is clusterwide
kubectl --context us-east get ccnp restrict-db-cross-cluster
kubectl --context eu-west get ccnp restrict-db-cross-cluster
✓

✅ Verify — Network Policy Enforced Across Both Clusters

CCNP restrict-db-cross-cluster is applied on both clusters. Remote eu-west pods can no longer bypass the policy — only pods with tier=api or tier=web labels can reach the db service across clusters. Hubble shows DROPPED verdicts for unauthorized cross-cluster db access.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
CNP applied locally → blocks local only
②
Remote pods bypass local CNP → no enforcement
③
Check CCNP → not deployed, CNP is cluster-scoped
④
Create CCNP on both clusters → cross-cluster enforcement
⑤
Remote unauthorized traffic now DROPPED

Tenet: Network policies are not synced across Cluster Mesh. Each cluster enforces its own policies independently. For cross-cluster enforcement, apply policies on ALL clusters where traffic originates or terminates. Use CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (CCNP) for consistent cluster-wide rules. CCNP applies to all namespaces and, when deployed on all clusters, provides consistent cross-cluster policy enforcement.

Fix Cluster Mesh Identity Conflict Between Clusters

The Problem: After connecting clusters, you notice identity conflicts — pods with the same labels in different clusters receive different numeric identities. Hubble shows incorrect policy verdicts. Your job: fix the identity allocation to ensure consistent identities across clusters.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cluster Mesh connected but identity conflicts exist
cilium clustermesh status
# Both clusters: OK

# Deploy same app in both clusters
for ctx in us-east eu-west; do
  kubectl --context $ctx create namespace anihpj
  kubectl --context $ctx create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=web
done

# ❌ BUG: Same labels → different numeric identities across clusters
kubectl --context us-east exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium identity list | grep anihpj
# 128    app=anihpj,tier=web    (us-east)
kubectl --context eu-west exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium identity list | grep anihpj
# 256    app=anihpj,tier=web    (eu-west)    ← Different identity!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cluster Mesh connected: cilium clustermesh status → OK ✅
✓2. Same labels in both clusters: kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels → app=anihpj,tier=web ✅
✗3. Different numeric identities: cilium identity list | grep anihpj → us-east: 128, eu-west: 256 — mismatch! ❌
✗4. Cross-cluster policy inconsistent: policy allowing identity 128 on us-east doesn't match identity 256 on eu-west ❌
✗5. Identity-based policy broken: policies referencing pod labels resolve to different numeric IDs per cluster ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check identity allocation mode: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep identity-allocation-mode
→ identity-allocation-mode: crd — each cluster independently allocates numeric identities from its own pool; no coordination across clusters
2Verify Cluster Mesh identity sync: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium bpf identity list | grep
→ Remote cluster identities are prefixed differently — Cluster Mesh does not unify local identity pools by default
3Check if cluster-pool identity mode would help: cilium config | grep cluster-pool
→ identity-allocation-mode could be set to 'kvstore' with shared etcd to coordinate identity allocation globally, but this requires external etcd setup
4Compare identity labels vs numeric IDs: kubectl get ciliumidentity -A | grep anihpj
→ Each cluster has its own CiliumIdentity CRDs with different numeric IDs — the identity-to-label mapping is local; Cluster Mesh propagates identities but doesn't unify them
5Root cause identified: CRD-based identity allocation assigns numeric IDs independently per cluster
→ When identity-allocation-mode=crd, each Cilium agent independently allocates a numeric identity for a label set. Since clusters don't coordinate identity allocation, the same labels get different numbers. For unified identities, either: 1) Use kvstore mode with shared etcd (global identity pool), or 2) Reference policies by labels (not numeric IDs), which Cilium resolves locally per cluster
🔧

🔧 Fix — Policies Work Across Clusters

BASH — policies work across clusters 
# Fix 1: Use label-based policies instead of identity-based
# Policies already use matchLabels — Cilium resolves per-cluster
# The numeric identity difference is cosmetic for label-based policies

# Fix 2 (for production): Switch to kvstore identity mode
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set identityAllocationMode=kvstore \
  --set etcd.enabled=true \
  --set etcd.endpoints[0]=https://shared-etcd.internal:2379

# Fix 3: Verify consistent identities after switch
for ctx in us-east eu-west; do
  kubectl --context $ctx exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium identity list | grep anihpj
done

# Important: label-based policies work fine even with different numeric IDs
# The numeric ID difference is only a problem for policies using toCIDRSet or identity-based rules
✓

✅ Verify — Label-Based Policies Enforced Consistently

Label-based CiliumNetworkPolicies work correctly across clusters despite different numeric identities. Cilium resolves matchLabels to the appropriate local numeric identity in each cluster. Cross-cluster traffic is correctly allowed/denied based on labels. For production, identityAllocationMode=kvstore with shared etcd ensures globally consistent numeric identities.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Same labels → different numeric IDs per cluster
②
identity-allocation-mode: crd → local pools
③
Label-based policies still work (resolve locally)
④
For unified IDs → switch to kvstore mode
⑤
Policies enforce correctly despite numeric differences

Tenet: Numeric identity differences across clusters are expected with CRD mode and generally don't break policies. Cilium resolves matchLabels to the local numeric identity in each cluster. Policies using labels work correctly. Only policies that reference numeric identities directly (rare) would be affected. For globally consistent numeric IDs, use identityAllocationMode=kvstore with a shared etcd cluster — this coordinates identity allocation across the mesh.

$ kubectl --context eu-west exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium identity list | grep "tier=web" 256 k8s:app=anihpj k8s:tier=web k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace=anihpj ← eu-west: 256 — DIFFERENT!

The Problem: You configure Egress Gateway to route anihpj outbound traffic through a specific node, but traffic exits from random nodes instead of the gateway node. External services see varying source IPs. Your job: fix the Egress Gateway to enforce consistent source IP masquerading.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Enable Egress Gateway on Cilium
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \

# Configure Egress NAT policy for anihpj
cat > egress-policy.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-egress
spec:
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
  destinationCIDRs:
  - "0.0.0.0/0"
  egressGateway:
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        egress-gateway: "true"
    egressIP: 203.0.113.10
EOF
kubectl apply -f egress-policy.yaml

# Label gateway node

# Deploy anihpj

# Returns node-2 IP (not gateway node-1 IP)!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Egress Gateway enabled: cilium config | grep egress-gateway → enabled ✅
✓2. Gateway node labeled: kubectl get nodes -l egress-gateway=true → worker-1 ✅
✗3. Traffic exits wrong node: curl ifconfig.me → returns random node IP, not gateway egressIP ❌
✗4. Source IP not masqueraded: egressIP 203.0.113.10 not used — pod's original IP visible ❌
✗5. Gateway policy not enforcing: cilium egress-gateway status → 0 active policies, 0 matched endpoints ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Egress Gateway policy status: kubectl get cegp -A
→ Policy exists but CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy status shows '0 matched' — the podSelector may not match any pods
2Verify pod labels match the policy selector: kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels
→ Pods have app=anihpj — but the policy uses matchLabels: {app: anihpj} which should match; check if the policy is in the correct namespace
3Check if the policy is namespace-scoped: kubectl get cegp anihpj-egress -o yaml | grep -E 'namespace|podSelector'
→ CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy is cluster-scoped (not namespaced) — but podSelector needs namespaceSelector to target specific namespaces or use matchExpressions
4Verify gateway node has the egress IP configured: kubectl get node worker-1 -o yaml | grep egress-gateway
→ Node has label but egressIP 203.0.113.10 may not be assigned to the node's network interface — the IP must exist on the gateway node
5Root cause identified: Egress Gateway policy missing namespace selector; gateway IP not on node interface
→ Egress Gateway requires: 1) Policy must specify BOTH podSelector AND namespaceSelector (or empty namespaceSelector {} for all namespaces), 2) The egressIP must be assigned to the gateway node's network interface (secondary IP or loopback alias), and 3) The gateway node must have IP forwarding enabled for the egress IP to be used as source
🔧

🔧 Fix — Egress Gateway Enforcing

BASH — egress gateway enforcing 
# Fix 1: Add namespace selector to the policy
kubectl patch cegp anihpj-egress --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"selectors":[{"namespaceSelector":{"matchLabels":{"kubernetes.io/metadata.name":"anihpj"}},"podSelector":{"matchLabels":{"app":"anihpj"}}}]}}'

# Fix 2: Add the egress IP to the gateway node
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ip addr add 203.0.113.10/32 dev eth0

# Fix 3: Enable IP forwarding on gateway node
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# Fix 4: Verify policy activates
cilium egress-gateway status
✓

✅ Verify — Traffic Exits via Gateway Node with Correct IP

All anihpj outbound traffic now exits through worker-1 with source IP 203.0.113.10. cilium egress-gateway status shows active policy with matched endpoints. curl ifconfig.me from any anihpj pod returns the consistent egress IP.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Egress policy created → traffic exits random nodes
②
Check policy → 0 matched endpoints
③
Missing namespaceSelector in policy
④
Add namespaceSelector + configure egressIP on node
⑤
All traffic exits via gateway with consistent IP

Tenet: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy needs both podSelector AND namespaceSelector (even if namespaceSelector is empty {} for all namespaces). Without namespaceSelector, the policy doesn't match any pods. The egressIP must be configured on the gateway node's interface — Cilium doesn't auto-assign it. IP forwarding must be enabled on the gateway node for NAT to work correctly.

Fix Egress Gateway Source IP Not Being Masqueraded

The Problem: Egress Gateway routes traffic through the gateway node, but the source IP is the pod IP, not the egress IP. External services reject traffic from private pod IPs. Your job: fix source IP masquerading so outbound traffic uses the gateway's egress IP.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Egress Gateway policy created, traffic flows through gateway node
# but source IP is still the pod IP

kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s http://httpbin.org/ip
# {"origin": "10.0.1.15"}    ← Pod IP, not egress IP! External services reject private IPs

# Check if masquerading is working
kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i masquerade
# "Egress Gateway masquerading: disabled"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Egress Gateway policy active: cilium egress-gateway status → policy matched ✅
✓2. Traffic routed via gateway: packets exit through gateway node ✅
✗3. Source IP not masqueraded: curl httpbin.org/ip → returns pod IP (10.0.x), not egress IP ❌
✗4. External services reject traffic: private pod IPs (10.0.x) dropped by external firewalls ❌
✗5. Masquerade not enabled: cilium config | grep masquerade → enable-ip-masq-agent: false ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check masquerading configuration: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep -A3 masquerade
→ enable-ip-masq-agent: "false" — IP masquerading is disabled; the egress gateway routes traffic but does not NAT the source IP
2Verify egress masquerade interface: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep egress-masquerade
→ egress-masquerade-interfaces not set — Cilium doesn't know which interface to use for source NAT on the gateway node
3Check if the gateway node can SNAT correctly: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING | grep MASQUERADE
→ No MASQUERADE rule for egress traffic — Cilium relies on BPF-based masquerading, not iptables; BPF masquerading must be explicitly enabled
4Verify BPF masquerade is enabled: cilium config | grep bpf-masquerade
→ bpf-masquerade: false — BPF-based masquerading is the most efficient; without it, fallback to iptables may not be configured
5Root cause identified: IP masquerading is disabled — traffic is routed but source IP is not rewritten
→ Egress Gateway routing and SNAT are separate features. The gateway policy routes traffic through a specific node, but without masquerading enabled, the source IP remains the pod IP. Enable BPF masquerade and specify the egress interface to rewrite source IP to the gateway node's egress IP
🔧

🔧 Fix — Source IP Masqueraded

BASH — source ip masqueraded 
# Fix 1: Enable BPF masquerading
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set bpf.masquerade=true \
  --set egressMasqueradeInterfaces=eth0

# Fix 2: Configure IP masquerade agent for egress
kubectl patch cm -n kube-system cilium-config \
  --patch '{"data":{"enable-ip-masq-agent":"true"}}'

# Fix 3: Restart Cilium agents to pick up masquerade config
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status ds/cilium -n kube-system

# Fix 4: Verify source IP is now masqueraded
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s http://httpbin.org/ip
✓

✅ Verify — Outbound Traffic Uses Gateway Egress IP

All anihpj outbound traffic now exits with source IP 203.0.113.10 (the egress IP). curl httpbin.org/ip returns the egress IP, not the pod IP. BPF masquerading is active on the eth0 interface. External services accept traffic from the routable egress IP.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Traffic routed via gateway but source IP unchanged
②
enable-ip-masq-agent: false
③
BPF masquerade not enabled
④
Enable BPF masquerade + set egress interface
⑤
Source IP rewritten to egress IP

Tenet: Egress Gateway routing (which node) and SNAT (source IP rewrite) are separate. The policy controls routing; masquerading controls IP rewriting. Enable bpf.masquerade=true for efficient BPF-based SNAT. Set egressMasqueradeInterfaces to the interface that has the egress IP. Without masquerading, the pod's private IP (10.0.x) leaks to external networks and gets dropped.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s http://httpbin.org/ip {"origin": "10.0.1.15"} ← Pod private IP — external services reject this!
$ cilium config | grep -E "masquerade|egress" enable-ip-masq-agent false bpf-masquerade false ← Both disabled!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s http://httpbin.org/ip {"origin": "203.0.113.10"} ✅ Egress IP — external services accept!
$ cilium config | grep -E "masquerade|egress" enable-ip-masq-agent true bpf-masquerade true enable-bpf-masquerade true ✅ Masquerading active!

🧪 SCENARIO S83 — Category 6: Cluster Mesh

Configure Egress NAT Policy for anihpj to Use Specific IP

The Problem: You need different anihpj components to use different egress IPs. The web tier should use one public IP, the api tier another. But the current Egress Gateway policy applies the same IP to all pods. Your job: create per-tier egress NAT policies with specific source IPs.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Current: Single egress policy for all anihpj pods
cat > single-egress.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-egress
spec:
  selectors:
  - namespaceSelector: {}
    podSelector:
      matchLabels: {app: anihpj}
  destinationCIDRs: ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  egressGateway:
    nodeSelector: {egress-gateway: "true"}
    egressIP: 203.0.113.10
EOF

# ❌ BUG: All pods share the same egress IP — can't differentiate by tier
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s ifconfig.me
# 203.0.113.10
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/api -- curl -s ifconfig.me
# 203.0.113.10    ← Same IP! Need different IPs per tier
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Egress Gateway enabled and working: cilium egress-gateway status → active policies ✅
✓2. Traffic masqueraded correctly: curl ifconfig.me → returns egress IP ✅
✗3. All pods share same IP: curl ifconfig.me from web and api → both return 203.0.113.10 ❌
✗4. Cannot differentiate traffic by source: external API rate limiting treats all anihpj pods as one client ❌
✗5. Single policy for all pods: no per-tier egress NAT — web and api need separate egress IPs ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if multiple policies can coexist: kubectl get cegp -A
→ Currently one policy — Cilium supports multiple CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy resources; each can target different podSelectors with different egress IPs
2Create per-tier policies with different selectors: For web tier: podSelector: {tier: web}; For api tier: podSelector: {tier: api}
→ Each policy needs a unique name and different podSelector to target specific tiers
3Verify the gateway node has multiple egress IPs: ip addr show eth0 | grep inet
→ Only 203.0.113.10 configured — need to add 203.0.113.11 for the second tier's egress IP
4Check if policies overlap correctly: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy with overlapping podSelectors uses first-match semantics; more specific selectors should be listed first
→ Policy order matters — if a catch-all policy matches first, more specific policies are ignored; create tier-specific policies with higher priority
5Root cause identified: Single catch-all policy — need multiple policies with per-tier selectors and egress IPs
→ Cilium supports multiple Egress Gateway policies with different selectors. Create separate policies for web and api tiers with their own podSelectors, egressIPs, and (optionally) different gateway nodes. Add the additional egress IPs to the gateway node's interface
🔧

🔧 Fix — Per-Tier Egress IPs

BASH — per-tier egress ips 
# Fix 1: Add second egress IP to gateway node
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ip addr add 203.0.113.11/32 dev eth0

# Fix 2: Create per-tier egress policies
cat > web-egress.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-egress
spec:
  selectors:
  - namespaceSelector: {}
    podSelector:
      matchLabels: {app: anihpj, tier: web}
  destinationCIDRs: ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  egressGateway:
    nodeSelector: {egress-gateway: "true"}
    egressIP: 203.0.113.10
EOF

cat > api-egress.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-egress
spec:
  selectors:
  - namespaceSelector: {}
    podSelector:
      matchLabels: {app: anihpj, tier: api}
  destinationCIDRs: ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  egressGateway:
    nodeSelector: {egress-gateway: "true"}
    egressIP: 203.0.113.11
EOF

kubectl delete cegp anihpj-egress
kubectl apply -f web-egress.yaml -f api-egress.yaml
✓

✅ Verify — Web and API Use Different Egress IPs

Web pods now exit with 203.0.113.10. API pods exit with 203.0.113.11. cilium egress-gateway status shows 2 active policies with separate endpoint matches. External services can differentiate traffic and apply per-tier rate limiting.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Single egress policy → all pods same IP
②
Need per-tier egress IPs for web and api
③
Multiple CEGPs supported with different selectors
④
Add second egress IP + create per-tier policies
⑤
Web→203.0.113.10, API→203.0.113.11

Tenet: Create separate CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy resources for different workload tiers. Each policy specifies its own podSelector (using more specific labels like tier=web vs tier=api) and egressIP. The gateway node must have all egress IPs configured on its interface. Delete any catch-all policy that would match all pods before the tier-specific policies.

$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/api -- curl -s ifconfig.me 203.0.113.10 ← Same IP as web — can't differentiate!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s ifconfig.me 203.0.113.10 ✅ Web tier egress IP
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/api -- curl -s ifconfig.me 203.0.113.11 ✅ API tier egress IP — different!

🧪 SCENARIO S84 — Category 6: Cluster Mesh

Debug Cluster Mesh Performance Degradation Under Load

The Problem: Under high traffic load, cross-cluster latency spikes and connections drop. Cluster Mesh performance degrades significantly when anihpj scales to 50+ pods. Your job: diagnose the performance bottleneck and optimize Cluster Mesh for production load.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal 
# Cluster Mesh working but performance degrades under load
cilium clustermesh status
# Both clusters: OK

# Scale anihpj to 50 pods
kubectl scale deployment web -n anihpj --replicas=50

# ❌ BUG: Cross-cluster latency spikes, connections drop
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' \
  http://api-service.anihpj.svc.global
# 2.5s, 5.1s, timeout — latency spikes under load!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cluster Mesh connected: cilium clustermesh status → OK ✅
✓2. Cross-cluster services resolve: nslookup api-service.anihpj.svc.global → resolves ✅
✗3. Latency spikes under load: curl -w '%{time_total}' → 2-5 seconds, intermittent timeouts ❌
✗4. Connections dropped: TCP connections to remote cluster services fail under high concurrency ❌
✗5. Cilium agent CPU spikes: kubectl top pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → CPU 80%+ on agents handling cross-cluster traffic ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check tunnel MTU for cross-cluster traffic: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ip link show cilium_vxlan | grep mtu
→ MTU 1450 — VXLAN tunnel adds 50 bytes overhead; with cross-cluster WAN links (typically 1500 MTU), fragmentation causes latency spikes
2Check Hubble flow rate under load: hubble observe --cluster anihpj-eu --output json | jq -r '.flow.traffic_direction' | sort | uniq -c
→ High drop rate during load — the tunnel bandwidth between clusters may be saturated or the etcd sync is falling behind
3Verify etcd sync performance: etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
→ etcd db size growing rapidly — large number of identities and endpoints being synced; etcd compaction may be needed
4Check CiliumEndpointSlice count: kubectl get ces -A --no-headers | wc -l
→ 100+ CES objects — with 50 pods per cluster, CES reduces API load but etcd sync still carries full endpoint state across clusters
5Root cause identified: Tunnel MTU mismatch, etcd sync overhead, and missing performance tuning
→ Cross-cluster performance degrades due to: 1) MTU mismatch causing packet fragmentation on WAN links, 2) etcd sync overhead proportional to endpoint count — each new pod triggers identity and endpoint sync across the mesh, 3) No connection-level load balancing — all cross-cluster traffic may funnel through a single tunnel endpoint, and 4) Missing affinity configuration causing unnecessary cross-cluster hops
🔧

🔧 Fix — Performance Optimized

BASH — performance optimized 
# Fix 1: Adjust MTU for cross-cluster WAN links
cilium config set mtu 1400  # Account for VXLAN + WAN overhead
cilium config set tunnel-port 8472

# Fix 2: Reduce etcd sync overhead with fewer, larger sync intervals
cilium config set clustermesh-sync-interval 60s

# Fix 3: Enable service affinity to prefer local backends
kubectl annotate svc -n anihpj api-service \
  io.cilium/service-affinity=local --overwrite

# Fix 4: Verify performance improvement
for i in $(seq 10); do
  kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' \
    http://api-service.anihpj.svc.global
done
✓

✅ Verify — Cross-Cluster Latency Under 50ms

Cross-cluster latency is under 50ms even with 50+ pods. MTU adjusted for WAN overhead eliminates fragmentation. Service affinity prefers local backends reducing cross-cluster hops. etcd sync interval increased to reduce control plane load. Hubble shows consistent FORWARDED flows with normal latency.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
50 pods → latency spikes 2-5s
②
Check MTU → 1450 causes fragmentation on WAN
③
etcd sync overhead per endpoint
④
Reduce MTU → enable affinity → increase sync interval
⑤
Latency <50ms under load

Tenet: Cluster Mesh performance tuning is critical at scale. Key optimizations: 1) MTU adjustment — VXLAN + WAN = 100 bytes overhead; set MTU to 1400 or lower, 2) Service affinity — prefer local backends to avoid cross-cluster hops when possible, 3) etcd sync interval — increase from default to reduce control plane overhead at scale, and 4) Monitor etcd DB size — compact regularly to prevent performance degradation.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ for i in $(seq 5); do kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total} " http://api-service.anihpj.svc.global; done 2.451 5.103 1.892 timeout 3.214 ← 2-5s latency + timeout under load!
$ kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- ip link show cilium_vxlan | grep mtu vxlan id 2 local 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 srcport 0 0 dstport 8472 mtu 1450 ← Too high for WAN!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ for i in $(seq 5); do kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/web -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total} " http://api-service.anihpj.svc.global; done 0.032 0.028 0.045 0.031 0.029 ✅ All under 50ms!
$ kubectl get svc -n anihpj api-service -o yaml | grep service-affinity io.cilium/service-affinity: local ✅ Local backends preferred!

🧪 SCENARIO S85 — Category 7: eBPF

Inspect Cilium eBPF Programs Loaded on anihpj Node with bpftool

The Problem: You need to inspect the eBPF programs Cilium loaded on a node running anihpj pods, but bpftool commands return empty output. Your job: use bpftool correctly to list, dump, and analyze Cilium's eBPF programs and maps on the node.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal
# Deploy anihpj on a Cilium node
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment api -n anihpj --port=80

# ❌ BUG: bpftool shows nothing
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- bpftool prog list
# (empty output — no programs listed)

# Try on the node directly
bpftool prog list
# (empty — bpftool needs root or CAP_BPF)
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → Running ✅
✓2. anihpj pods deployed: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → Running ✅
✗3. bpftool inside agent: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- bpftool prog list → empty — no Cilium programs listed! ❌
✗4. bpftool on node: bpftool prog list → empty or "Operation not permitted" ❌
✗5. Cannot see any BPF maps either: bpftool map list → no BPF maps visible ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if bpftool is installed on the node: which bpftool || apt list --installed | grep bpftool
→ bpftool not installed — it's a separate package (linux-tools-common) that must be installed explicitly
2Check if running with sufficient privileges: sudo bpftool prog list | head -5
→ With sudo, programs appear — bpftool requires CAP_BPF, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, or root to inspect kernel eBPF objects
3Use bpftool with proper mount namespace: nsenter -t $(pgrep cilium-agent) -m bpftool prog list
→ Cilium programs live in the agent's mount namespace — accessing from host namespace requires nsenter to the agent's PID
4List Cilium-specific programs by tag prefix: bpftool prog list | grep -E 'cilium|from-container|to-container|from-overlay|to-host'
→ Cilium programs are tagged with names like 'cil_from_container', 'cil_to_container', 'cil_to_overlay' — filtering reveals them
5Root cause identified: bpftool requires root/CAP_BPF and correct mount namespace
→ eBPF programs are kernel objects protected by Linux capabilities. bpftool must run as root (or with CAP_BPF+CAP_SYS_ADMIN) to enumerate programs. On the node, use sudo. Inside Cilium agent pod, the container has these capabilities. For node-level inspection, use nsenter to the Cilium agent's PID mount namespace since eBPF filesystem (bpffs) is mounted per-namespace
🔧

🔧 Fix — bpftool Lists Cilium eBPF Programs

BASH — inspect BPF programs with sudo bpftool
# Fix 1: Install bpftool on the node
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y linux-tools-common linux-tools-$(uname -r)

# Fix 2: Run bpftool with sudo to list all eBPF programs
sudo bpftool prog list

# Fix 3: Filter Cilium programs only
sudo bpftool prog list | grep -E 'cil|from-container|to-container'

# Fix 4: Inside Cilium agent pod (already has caps)
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- bpftool prog list

# Fix 5: From host, enter agent's namespace
CILIUM_PID=$(pgrep -f cilium-agent | head -1)
sudo nsenter -t $CILIUM_PID -m bpftool prog list
✓

✅ Verify — Cilium eBPF Programs Visible with bpftool

Running sudo bpftool prog list on the node shows all eBPF programs, including Cilium's datapath programs tagged with names like cil_from_container, cil_to_container, and cil_to_overlay. Each program shows its BPF type (sched_cls, xdp, cgroup_skb), ID, and tag hash. The anihpj pod's veth interface has Cilium programs attached at the TC hook.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
bpftool prog list → empty
②
Check: bpftool not installed
③
Check: needs sudo/CAP_BPF
④
Check: wrong mount namespace
⑤
Install bpftool → sudo → nsenter → programs visible

Tenet: eBPF programs are kernel objects — they are NOT visible to unprivileged users. Always use sudo bpftool on the host or run inside the Cilium agent pod. Cilium programs use TC (sched_cls) hooks on veth interfaces and XDP hooks on physical interfaces. Key program names: cil_from_container (ingress from pod), cil_to_container (egress to pod), cil_to_overlay (VXLAN/Geneve encapsulation), cil_from_network (from physical network).

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ bpftool prog list (empty — no output)
$ which bpftool bpftool not found ← Not installed!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo bpftool prog list | head -10 89: sched_cls name cil_from_container tag 6deef7357e7b4530 loaded_at 2025-12-16T12:00:00 uid 0 xlated 240B jited 152B memlock 4096B 92: sched_cls name cil_to_container tag abc123def456 loaded_at 2025-12-16T12:00:00 uid 0 xlated 312B jited 198B memlock 4096B ✅ Cilium programs visible!
$ sudo bpftool prog list | grep -c cil 8 ← 8 Cilium eBPF programs loaded on this node

# Verify cleanup

Debug eBPF Verifier Rejecting Cilium Program on Old Kernel

The Problem: After upgrading Cilium on a node with kernel 5.4, the eBPF verifier rejects Cilium's programs. The Cilium agent logs show verifier errors and anihpj pods on that node lose connectivity. Your job: diagnose why the verifier rejects programs and fix the issue.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal
# Node with kernel 5.4 — Cilium agent fails after upgrade
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1

# ❌ BUG: Cilium agent logs show verifier rejection
kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i verifier
# "BPF program rejected by verifier: back-edge from insn 142 to 47"
# "load program: invalid argument (possible verifier complexity issue on older kernels)"

kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# web-xxx   0/1   Pending   ← No CNI for this pod!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium agent started: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → Init:Error/Running ✅
✓2. Other nodes fine: other nodes with kernel 5.10+ run Cilium OK ✅
✗3. Agent logs show verifier errors: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium → "BPF program rejected by verifier" ❌
✗4. anihpj pods Pending on this node: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide → Pods scheduled to bad node are stuck Pending ❌
✗5. Check kernel version: uname -r → 5.4.0 — too old for new Cilium eBPF features ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check kernel version: uname -r
→ 5.4.0-110-generic — Cilium v1.16 requires kernel 5.10+ for full feature set; the verifier in 5.4 has complexity limits that reject newer Cilium programs
2Check verifier error details: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -A3 'verifier'
→ back-edge from insn 142 to 47 — the program has a bounded loop, but kernel 5.4 verifier rejects ALL loops (loop support added in 5.3, improved in 5.8+)
3Check verifier log for complexity: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep 'processed.*insn'
→ processed 1000000 insns (limit 1000000) — the verifier hit its complexity limit; Cilium's newer programs are larger and exceed the 5.4 verifier's state pruning limits
4Check if CO-RE is available: ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux 2>/dev/null
→ BTF not available — without BTF, Cilium falls back to non-CO-RE mode which generates more complex BPF programs that the old verifier rejects
5Root cause identified: Kernel 5.4 verifier has lower complexity limits and stricter loop handling
→ eBPF verifier limits increased significantly across kernel versions: 5.4 allows 1M processed instructions, 5.10 allows 1M with better state pruning, 5.15+ allows 1M+ with bounded loops. Cilium v1.16 programs are optimized for kernels 5.10+ and may exceed 5.4 verifier limits. Without BTF for CO-RE, the fallback programs are even more complex
🔧

🔧 Fix — Verifier Accepts Cilium Programs

BASH — upgrade kernel to 5.10+ for verifier support
# Fix 1: Upgrade kernel to 5.10+ (recommended for Cilium v1.16+)
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y linux-generic-hwe-22.04
sudo reboot

# Fix 2: If kernel upgrade not possible, downgrade Cilium
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system \
  --version 1.15.0 \
  --reuse-values

# Fix 3: Cordon old-kernel node so anihpj pods don't schedule there
kubectl cordon 
kubectl drain  --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# Fix 4: Verify verifier limits after kernel upgrade
cat /proc/sys/kernel/unprivileged_bpf_disabled
sysctl net.core.bpf_jit_enable=1  # Ensure JIT is enabled
✓

✅ Verify — eBPF Verifier Passes on Upgraded Kernel

After upgrading to kernel 5.10+, the eBPF verifier accepts Cilium's programs. Agent logs show BPF program loaded successfully instead of verifier errors. anihpj pods on the node transition from Pending to Running. bpftool prog list | grep cil shows all Cilium programs loaded on the node.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Agent logs → verifier rejection
②
Kernel 5.4 → verifier complexity limit hit
③
No BTF → non-CO-RE programs too complex
④
Upgrade kernel to 5.10+ → restart Cilium
⑤
Verifier passes → anihpj pods Running

Tenet: The eBPF verifier is a kernel component that validates BPF programs before loading. Each kernel version has different verifier capabilities. Key milestones: 5.3: bounded loops, 5.8: improved state pruning, 5.10: 1M insn limit with BTF/CO-RE, 5.15: significantly higher limits. Cilium targets 5.10+ for full functionality. The cilium kernel-check command validates each node against feature requirements.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i verifier level=fatal msg="BPF program rejected by verifier" error="back-edge from insn 142 to 47" subsys=datapath-loader level=fatal msg="load program: invalid argument" error="verifier complexity limit reached"
$ uname -r 5.4.0-110-generic ← Too old for Cilium v1.16 programs
$ ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux ls: cannot access '/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux': No such file or directory ← No BTF!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ uname -r 5.15.0-91-generic ✅ Kernel upgraded!
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep "loaded" level=info msg="BPF program loaded successfully" program=cil_from_container level=info msg="BPF program loaded successfully" program=cil_to_container ✅ Verifier passed!
$ sudo bpftool prog list | grep cil | wc -l 8 ✅ All 8 Cilium programs loaded
🧹

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH — copy & paste to clean up
# Delete the namespace
kubectl delete namespace anihpj
# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj

Dump and Analyze BPF Policy Maps for anihpj Endpoints

The Problem: You need to inspect Cilium's BPF policy maps to understand why anihpj traffic is being dropped, but you cannot find or dump the policy maps. Your job: locate Cilium's pinned BPF maps, dump policy entries, and correlate them with anihpj endpoint identities.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal
# Deploy anihpj with a CNP that drops api→db
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true

cat > cnp-restrict.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels: {app: anihpj, tier: db}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels: {app: anihpj, tier: web}
    toPorts:
    - ports: [{port: "5432"}]
EOF
kubectl apply -f cnp-restrict.yaml

kubectl create deployment web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=web
kubectl create deployment api -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=api
kubectl create deployment db -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=db
kubectl expose deployment db -n anihpj --port=5432

# ❌ BUG: Cannot find policy maps
sudo bpftool map list | grep -i policy
# (empty — need to know map names/paths)
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. CNP applied: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj restrict-db → exists ✅
✓2. Traffic being dropped: hubble observe --verdict DROPPED → api→db:5432 DROPPED ✅
✗3. Cannot find policy maps: sudo bpftool map list | grep -i pol → too many maps, need Cilium-specific paths ❌
✗4. Generic bpftool map dump: bpftool map dump id → shows raw hex — unreadable without understanding Cilium's map structure ❌
✗5. No correlation to identity: map entries are opaque (identity IDs, not labels) — need Cilium CLI to decode ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Locate Cilium's BPF map pins: ls /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/ | grep cilium
→ Cilium pins its BPF maps under /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/ — policy maps are named cilium_policy_XXXXX where XXXXX is the endpoint ID
2Find an anihpj endpoint ID: kubectl get cep -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[0].status.id'
→ Endpoint ID 1234 — Cilium creates per-endpoint policy maps pinned with this ID
3Dump a specific policy map: sudo bpftool map dump pinned /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/cilium_policy_01234
→ Map entries show identity keys and policy action values (1=allow, 0=deny) — this is the ingress policy for endpoint 1234
4Use cilium-dbg to decode map entries: cilium-dbg bpf policy get 1234
→ cilium-dbg translates map entries into human-readable format: shows which identities are allowed/denied for the endpoint
5Root cause identified: BPF policy maps are pinned per-endpoint and require Cilium CLI for decoding
→ Cilium's BPF policy maps use numeric identity IDs as keys and policy decision IDs as values. Raw bpftool dump shows hex — you need cilium-dbg or cilium endpoint list to correlate endpoint IDs with pods and cilium-dbg bpf policy get to decode the actual allow/deny rules per identity
🔧

🔧 Fix — Policy Maps Dumped and Analyzed

BASH — use cilium-dbg to decode policy map entries
# Fix 1: List Cilium endpoints and their IDs
kubectl get cep -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,ID:.status.id,IDENTITY:.status.identity.id,IP:.status.networking.addressing[0].ipv4

# Fix 2: Use cilium-dbg to inspect policy for an endpoint
cilium-dbg bpf policy get 

# Fix 3: Dump the raw BPF policy map
sudo bpftool map dump pinned /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/cilium_policy_0

# Fix 4: Correlate identity IDs with labels
cilium-dbg identity list | grep -E "anihpj|reserved"

# Fix 5: Check which identities can reach an endpoint
cilium-dbg bpf policy get  --all
✓

✅ Verify — BPF Policy Maps Correlated with anihpj Endpoints

Using cilium-dbg bpf policy get <endpoint-id>, the BPF policy map for the db endpoint shows identity 128 (web) is ALLOWED on port 5432 and identity 256 (api) is DENIED — matching the CNP. Raw bpftool map dump confirms the same entries in hex format. The policy is correctly enforced at the eBPF level.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
bpftool map list → too many maps
②
Find Cilium's pinned maps under /sys/fs/bpf
③
Get endpoint IDs from CEP CRD
④
cilium-dbg bpf policy get → decoded
⑤
Policy map confirms CNP: web ALLOW, api DENY

Tenet: Cilium pins BPF maps at /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/ (for endpoint-specific maps) and /sys/fs/bpf/cilium/ (for global maps). Key maps: cilium_policy_XXXXX (per-endpoint policy), cilium_ct4_global (conntrack), cilium_lb4_services (service load balancing), cilium_ipcache (identity↔IP mapping). Always prefer cilium-dbg bpf over raw bpftool — it decodes Cilium's data structures.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo bpftool map list | wc -l 47 ← 47 BPF maps on the node — need to filter!
$ ls /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/ | grep cilium_policy cilium_policy_01234 cilium_policy_01235 cilium_policy_01236 ← Per-endpoint policy maps
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cilium-dbg bpf policy get 1234 DIRECTION IDENTITY PORT/PROTO ACTION Ingress 128 (web) 5432/TCP ALLOW Ingress 256 (api) 5432/TCP DENY ← CNP enforced! Ingress 0 (world) ANY DENY Egress 0 (world) ANY ALLOW ✅ Policy matches CNP!
$ sudo bpftool map dump pinned /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/cilium_policy_01234 | head -3 key: 80 00 00 00 value: 01 00 00 00 ← Identity 128 = ALLOW(1) key: 00 01 00 00 value: 00 00 00 00 ← Identity 256 = DENY(0) ✅ Raw hex matches decoded output!

Fix eBPF Map Full Error — Max Entries Reached for anihpj

The Problem: Cilium agent logs show BPF map full errors and new anihpj pods cannot get network connectivity. The conntrack or policy map has reached its maximum entry limit. Your job: identify which map is full, increase its max entries, and restore anihpj connectivity.
1

📋 Deploy the YAML (contains the bug)

BASH — copy & paste into Ubuntu terminal
# Deploy many anihpj pods to fill BPF maps
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj io.cilium/network-policy=true
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  kubectl create deployment anihpj-web-$i -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine -l app=anihpj,tier=web
done

# ❌ BUG: New pods stuck Pending or have no network
kubectl get pods -n anihpj | grep -c Running
# Only 75 Running — 25 stuck Pending or without IP

kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i "map full"
# "Cannot insert entry into BPF map: map is full (max_entries reached)"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✓1. Cilium running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium → Running ✅
✓2. 75 anihpj pods Running: kubectl get pods -n anihpj | grep Running | wc -l → 75 ✅
✗3. 25 pods stuck: kubectl get pods -n anihpj | grep -v Running → Pending/CrashLoopBackOff ❌
✗4. Agent logs show map full: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep "map full" → "Cannot insert entry: map is full" ❌
✗5. Check map sizes: bpftool map list -j | jq '.[] | {name, max_entries}' → conntrack map at 512K entries — full! ❌
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check which BPF map is full: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -B2 'map is full'
→ cilium_ct4_global (conntrack table) at 512K/512K entries — the default conntrack map size is insufficient for 100+ pods with active connections
2Check Cilium ConfigMap for map sizes: kubectl get cm -n kube-system cilium-config -o yaml | grep -i 'map\|bpf'
→ bpf-ct-global-any-max and bpf-policy-map-max not explicitly set — using defaults (512K conntrack, 16K policy)
3Count current conntrack entries: cilium-dbg bpf ct list global | wc -l
→ 512000 entries — the conntrack table is at absolute maximum; new connections cannot be tracked, so they are dropped or pods cannot get IPs
4Check if GC is running: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep -i 'garbage\|gc\|ct cleanup'
→ Conntrack GC is running but the churn rate from 100 pods exceeds GC cleanup rate — entries are created faster than they are cleaned
5Root cause identified: Default BPF map sizes are too small for large-scale deployments
→ Cilium's default BPF map sizes (512K for conntrack, 16K for policy, 64K for NAT) are sized for typical workloads. At 100+ pods with active connections, the conntrack table fills up. When a BPF map is full, Cilium cannot insert new entries — new connections fail and new pods cannot register endpoints. The fix is to increase map sizes via ConfigMap or Helm values
🔧

🔧 Fix — BPF Maps Resized

BASH — increase BPF map sizes via ConfigMap
# Fix 1: Increase conntrack map size (and other maps)
kubectl patch configmap -n kube-system cilium-config --type merge -p '{"data":{"bpf-ct-global-any-max":"1048576","bpf-ct-global-tcp-max":"524288","bpf-policy-map-max":"65536","bpf-nat-global-max":"524288"}}'

# Fix 2: Restart Cilium agents to recreate maps with new sizes
kubectl rollout restart ds/cilium -n kube-system
kubectl rollout status ds/cilium -n kube-system --timeout=300s

# Fix 3: Verify new map sizes
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- bpftool map list | grep -E "ct|policy|nat"

# Fix 4: If using Helm, set values permanently
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set bpf.ctGlobalAnyMax=1048576 \
  --set bpf.policyMapMax=65536
✓

✅ Verify — BPF Maps Have Sufficient Capacity for 100+ Pods

After increasing BPF map sizes via ConfigMap and restarting agents, the conntrack map has 1M entries (was 512K), policy map has 64K entries (was 16K). All 100 anihpj pods are Running with IPs. Agent logs show no more "map is full" errors. bpftool map list confirms the new max_entries values.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
100 pods → 25 stuck without network
②
Agent logs: map is full
③
Conntrack at 512K/512K → full
④
Increase bpf-ct-global-any-max to 1M
⑤
Restart agents → all 100 pods Running

Tenet: BPF maps are pre-allocated at agent startup. Key maps and recommended sizes for large clusters: Conntrack (ct) = number of active connections, Policy = number of policy rules × endpoints, NAT = number of NAT entries for services. Rule of thumb: conntrack = 10K × number of pods, policy = 1K × endpoints. All map sizes are configured via bpf-*-max Helm values or ConfigMap entries. Maps cannot be resized without agent restart.

📟 Command Outputs — Error State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium | grep "map is full" level=error msg="Cannot insert entry into BPF map: map is full" map-name=cilium_ct4_global max_entries=524288 current=524288 subsys=ct level=error msg="Failed to create CT entry for new flow"
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj --no-headers | grep -v Running | wc -l 25 ← 25 pods stuck due to full BPF maps
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- bpftool map list | grep ct 123: lru_hash name cilium_ct4_global flags 0x0 key 20B value 64B max_entries 1048576 memlock 134217728B ✅ 1M entries!
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj --no-headers | grep Running | wc -l 100 ✅ All pods Running!
🧹

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

kubectl delete namespace anihpj
# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj
